title: Data Center Late Fees Hit $5 Million or More Per Day, Spawning New Insurance
content: This spring, Mike Mathews, who leads the global digital infrastructure practice at insurance broker Marsh, raced to design a policy to protect a data center developer from a $1 million-a-day late fee. The developer’s tenant was demanding damages if electricity and facilities weren’t available on time during the first phase of a new gigawatt-scale facility. Mathews’ team arranged the novel coverage, a bespoke form of “delay-in-delivery” coverage just for data centers, only to see penalties escalate sharply in a matter of months: Tenants in new deals began asking for upwards of $5 million for each day of delay, citing even higher estimates of lost revenue.

title: Li battery manufacturing emissions could rise 10-fold by 2050, study warns – Batteries International
content: Manufacturing and supply-chain emissions from lithium ion batteries could increase more than 10-fold by 2050 as global demand rises — with cleaner production alone not enough to limit the impact, according to a University of Melbourne-led study. The study’s modelling found that over the same period, demand for LIBs used in electric cars, vans, buses, trucks and battery energy storage systems could rise 20-fold, fuelling the increase in supply-chain greenhouse gas emissions (GHG). The university said the study, released on October 16 and supported by researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the University of Sheffield, is one of the first detailed global assessments to examine both supply-side and demand-side factors. Published in Cell Press’ sustainability journal ‘ One Earth ’, the research, led by University of Melbourne associate professor Wen Li, found that cleaner production alone was not enough to mitigate the resulting annual LIB supply chain emissions. GHG emissions were quantified across four life cycle stages of LIBs through 2050 — battery material production, component production, battery manufacturing and end-of-life treatment, based on projected activity levels and GHG intensities for each stage. As the world deploys batteries faster than ever, these emissions could offset the very climate benefits batteries are meant to deliver, the study claims. “Cleaning up production on the supply side, such as switching battery chemistries, building greener factories, and recovering materials from used batteries, is the common response, but each of these levers has a practical ceiling, leaving it unclear whether cleaner production can outrun the rising demand.” While supply-side strategies lower GHG intensity substantially, cutting cumulative emissions by 3.5-4.7 gigatonnes of CO 2 -equivalent, they face mitigation limits from technical ceilings, deployment dynamics, and cross-strategy interactions. Demand-side strategies are essential to further constrain supply-chain emissions, unlocking 6-7.2 Gt CO 2 -eq of cumulative mitigation beyond what supply-side decarbonisation alone can achieve. Wen Li said while cleaner production helped, reducing demand was “another very large mitigation opportunity”. He said supply-side decarbonisation remained essential. Cleaner electricity was especially important and recycling increasingly valuable. However, without the additional measures tested, the global battery supply chain could generate around 19–23 billion tonnes CO₂-eq emissions through to 2050. “Combining ambitious supply- and demand-side strategies cuts this to around 9–12 billion tonnes, roughly half,” Wen Li said. Objectives for policymakers globally should not only ask how to make each battery cleaner but also interrogate how many batteries are sustainably viable to produce, replace, and process. Study lead and first author Haiwei Zhou, of the University of Melbourne’s Faculty of Engineering and Information Technology, said the team now hoped to improve the model’s regional resolution, as mining, refining, electricity and environmental pressures varied greatly between locations. “We also want to test whether the same supply-versus-demand dynamic appears in other rapidly growing clean-energy supply chains such as wind turbines and solar panels.” To see the full study online, click here . title: E-quipment highlight: the highest-rated mowers on Amazon are ELECTRIC (2026)
content:
Green Deals
Commercial EVs
Lawn mower
Electric Power Tools
Jo Borrás
| Oct 25 2026 - 1:01 am PT
Despite decades of market dominance, it seems like the days of loud, finicky, gas-powered mowers may finally be behind us; and I say that because –
for the second year in a row
– the highest-rated lawnmowers on Amazon won’t burn a drop of gas.
The latest round of dumb oil wars are ratcheting up fuel prices everywhere while, at the same time,
state and local governments continue to tightening restrictions on noise and small-engine emissions
. Combined, those things probably mean that your next lawn mower is more likely to plug in than fill up, whether you like it or not. The
news is that. in addition to being quieter, safer,
and not poisoning the air you breathe while you walk behind them
, electric laenmowers have come a long way in terms of power and performance in just a few years. So much so, in fact, that many of the highest-rated models on Amazon,
emphatic period
, are electric.
In putting this list together, we looked at the average star ratings of a number of lawn mowers on Amazon, focusing on products that had at least 2,000 reviews and a four-star average or higher, and found that (like last year) battery-electric units from EGO Power, Greenworks, and Worx were among the top-rated mowers, regardless of fuel type.
Here’s the rundown, in alphabetical order (by brand).
EGO POWER+ LM2112 21″ electric mower.
Over the past few years, the EGO POWER+ brand has staked a claim to being the gold standard for cordless lawn equipment, thanks to its high-voltage 56V battery platform and premium build quality.
The brand’s 21″ POWER+ LM2112 push mower currently carries a 4.5-star average rating from more than 2,200 Amazon reviews and an “Overall Pick” designation
That’s no surprise, given the LM2112’s 6 ft-lbs. of cutting torque (equivalent to a 150cc ICE), and up to 35 minutes of runtime (call it a suburban yard) from the included
56V 4.0 Ah li-ion battery
, three-in-one mulching, bagging and side-discharge capability. It also starts at the push of a button, folds for compact storage and skips the exhaust, maintenance, and oil changes that come along with a comparable gas mower.
Greenworks
Greenworks 40V 16″ push mower.
With an impressive 4.2-star rating after more than 12,000 verified reviews,
the Greenworks 40V 16″ push mower is in rare company among mowers of any kind on Amazon
. No surprise, given that the lightweight, cordless mower weighs just 37.5 lbs. and comes with a 4.0Ah battery and charger good for up to 40 minutes of runtime, making it ideal for homeowners with smaller yards who want to ditch gas without wrestling with a heavier machine.
The Greenpower’s 16″ cutting deck is designed for (if not limited to) compact lawns, with a five-position height adjustment and a two-in-one system offering you a choice of mulching (yes) or bagging (no) your lawn clippings.
For bigger, more demanding lawns,
Greenworks offers a 4.4-star push mower with a 21″ steel cutting deck that’s powered by an 80V brushless motor and ships with a pair of 2.0 Ah batteries good for up to 40 minutes of runtime with both batteries
. Three-in-one functionality for mulching, bagging, or side discharge is included, too, along with push-button starting, seven-position height adjustment, and a rapid charger that can get it back to work in about 30 minutes.
WORX 17″ battery-powered mower.
WORX’s 40V 17″ Power Share mower is another strong example of how electric lawn care can be both practical and affordable.
The WG743 mates a pair of 20V, 4.0 Ah batteries to deliver 40V of power
, and those same batteries work across the brand’s broader Power Share lineup of tools – a lineup that includes string trimmers, power drills, and more.
The WORX mower’s standout feature, though, is its “IntelliCut” technology that works a bit like traction control in your car, automatically increasing torque when the mower hits thicker grass (more traction) and backing off when it doesn’t need the extra power (when it detects wheelspin – or, in this case, cutting head spin). Factor in an intentionally lightweight design, seven-position cutting-height adjustment, and the
options for mulching or bagging, and you’ve got a versatile little mower for keeping a smaller lawn in shape.

title: 7 technologies the US military uses to stop hostile drones
content:
2. Coyote interceptor drones – Coyote 2C
Developed by RTX, the Coyote is a radar-guided interceptor designed to defeat hostile drones physically. It can be integrated into the Army’s fixed-site and mobile counter-UAS defenses, with kinetic and non-kinetic variants available. In January 2024, the Army awarded RTX a
$75 million contract
for 600 Coyote 2C interceptors, highlighting the effort to scale up defenses against small unmanned aircraft.
3. Vehicle-mounted guns with automated targeting – BLADE
The Ballistic Low Altitude Drone Engagement system adapts the Army’s existing remotely operated weapon stations to engage small drones. It combines automated detection and tracking with a gun-based response, offering a kinetic alternative to electronic warfare. During Project Flytrap 4.0 in Poland in August 2025, soldiers used BLADE on a Stryker to defeat multiple drones at reported ranges of 500–800 meters (0.3 to 0.5 mile).
4. Radio-frequency detection and electronic warfare – NINJA
The Air Force’s Negation of Improvised Non-State Joint Aerial Threats program uses radio-frequency signals associated with drones and their operators to detect, locate, identify, and help defeat threats. This approach can provide warning without relying solely on radar. A Congressional Research Service report noted that 99 Air Force locations had installed NINJA as of 2023 testimony. The effectiveness of electronic warfare depends on the target’s communications and operating characteristics.

title: 3D-printed ceramic wall fights heat with water, cools air by 12.5°F
content:
Global warming has become one of Earth’s biggest environmental challenges. To address this growing problem, nearly every nation in the world adopted the Paris Agreement in 2015, and pledged to keep global warming well below 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit (two degrees Celsius) above pre-industrial levels. The agreement also pushed for a lower limit of 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5 degrees Celsius).
But things didn’t go as planned. Greenhouse emissions remained high, fossil fuels continued to dominate the energy market, and countries eventually fell behind on their climate goals. By September 2026, even
the best-case scenario
pointed to a temperature rise of 3.1 to 3.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius).

title: Quantum memory uses sound to store qubits for computing
content:
Today’s quantum computers are built so that qubits function as both computational and storage units. This works at smaller scales, which we see today. However,
qubits are fragile
As quantum computers grow to include more qubits, this fragility becomes a bigger problem.
In large computations, many qubits must wait between operations, during which their quantum states can decay. This is where the dual role becomes a limitation. A qubit that needs to compute quickly has a strong connection to control signals, which also makes it susceptible to noise and less suitable for storing information for long periods of time.

title: 10 inventions from the US that transformed modern life
content:
1. The telephone
Alexander Graham Bell received a U.S. patent for his telephone in 1876, starting a new era of real-time voice communication. His device converted sound into electrical signals that could travel over wires and be converted back into speech.
Earlier inventors explored similar ideas, but Bell’s work made the telephone a practical technology. Its descendants now underpin
mobile communications
, internet calling, and the global telecommunications networks connecting billions of people.
2. The airplane
On December 17, 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright achieved the first successful powered, controlled, and sustained airplane flights at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Their achievement followed years of experimentation with gliders, propellers, and flight controls.
Wright Flyer
stayed airborne for only seconds during its first flight, but the underlying engineering principles helped make powered aviation practical. Aircraft subsequently transformed passenger travel, global trade, emergency response, and military operations, shrinking the practical distances between continents.

title: What happens to satellites when they run out of fuel in orbit
content: Running out of fuel might leave a car stranded, but a satellite keeps moving. Even with an empty tank, it can continue circling Earth long after its useful mission has ended.Fuel allows satellites to adjust their orbits, maintain their positions, and avoid potential collisions. Once it runs out, a spacecraft may still have electricity and working instruments, but lose the ability to make these maneuvers.What follows depends largely on altitude and whether operators prepared for retirement. Some satellites gradually return to Earth, while others remain in space long after they stop working.Fuel is for maneuveringA satellite does not need an engine running continuously to stay in orbit. Its forward motion carries it around Earth while gravity pulls it toward the planet. It is constantly falling, but moving sideways fast enough to keep missing the ground.Propellant helps change that motion. Thrusters can raise or lower an orbit, correct a satellite’s position, or move it away from a predicted collision.Without usable propellant, those options disappear unless another propulsion system or servicing spacecraft can help.However, an empty fuel tank does not automatically switch off the electronics. Most Earth-orbiting satellites draw electricity from solar panels, with batteries supplying power during periods without sunlight.Some can also use electrically powered reaction wheels or magnetic devices to control their orientation. Whether useful operations continue depends on the spacecraft’s design and mission requirements.The orbit decides what followsIn low Earth orbit, satellites encounter traces of the atmosphere. This creates drag, which gradually removes orbital energy and lowers their altitude.Without propulsion to counter that drag, a spacecraft can eventually descend into denser atmospheric layers. Heating and aerodynamic forces then cause it to break apart.The process has no fixed timeline. Altitude, spacecraft shape, mass, and atmospheric conditions all influence how long it takes. Solar activity can expand the upper atmosphere, increasing drag.Much of a satellite may burn up during reentry, although heat-resistant components can survive and reach the surface.Geostationary satellites operate much farther away, roughly 35,786 kilometers (22,236 miles) above the equator.Atmospheric drag there is negligible, so losing fuel does not send them quickly back to Earth. Instead, they can drift away from their assigned positions while remaining in space.Retirement starts before fuel runs outWaiting until the tank is empty can leave operators unable to dispose of a satellite safely.For spacecraft closer to Earth, controllers can use remaining propellant to lower the orbit and accelerate reentry. Some missions can target a remote ocean area through a controlled descent.Geostationary satellites are generally raised into graveyard orbits above the operational region. This also requires fuel, which must be reserved before routine operations exhaust the supply.Operators then make stored energy sources safe through a process called passivation. This can involve releasing residual propellant, relieving pressure, and discharging or disconnecting batteries to reduce the risk of accidental explosions.If a satellite loses maneuvering capability before retirement, it can become a persistent collision hazard. Its mission may be over, but other spacecraft still have to share space with it.

title: Scientists uncover ant wars along California's 600-mile supercolony
content: In Southern California, rival ants warred at the borders of their massive supercolonies for years, with casualties soaring into the millions. Native to South America, Argentine ants (Linepithema humile) have spread worldwide through international trade.This species has an unusual form of social organization known as unicoloniality, in which ants from different nests cooperate rather than fight.“Some species of ants possess an unusual form of social organization in which aggression among nests is absent,” researchers stated in a recent study. “This type of social organization, called unicoloniality, has been studied in only a handful of species and its evolutionary origins remain unclear.”However, when these ants found new territory, they sometimes formed enormous supercolonies. One in coastal California extends approximately 620 miles long, while several smaller supercolonies occupied surrounding territories. With relatively low genetic diversity, they recognized one another from different nests and knew they belonged to the same group. However, when ants from rival supercolonies met, cooperation turned to aggression. Their borders are “well-defined”Researchers identified 16 contact zones between three supercolonies. Over six months, they monitored nine of them weekly. They described these boundaries as “abrupt and well-defined” in a new study published in Molecular Ecology. The team documented “consistent and intense intercolony aggression that resulted in variable, but often large, levels of worker mortality.”According to IFLScience, researchers observed fighting at 40 percent of site visits, with an average of 15,000 worker ants killed per battle. Near Lake Hodges, researchers estimated that at least 15 million ants died during the six-month observation period.Using microsatellites, they examined genetic differences between ants within the same supercolony and those in competing groups. Differentiation was substantially lower within supercolonies than between them.“…Levels of aggression and genetic differentiation were significantly correlated, but no relationship existed between geographic distance and either intraspecific aggression or genetic differentiation,” the researchers wrote.Genetic differences were associated with aggression. They found high levels of gene flow within supercolonies, but little to no gene flow between them, suggesting that rival supercolonies remained genetically distinct even after prolonged contact along their borders. A territorial war with no clear winnerDespite the millions of casualties, the boundaries showed little movement during the researchers’ observation period, akin to a prolonged stalemate in human wars, according to IFLScience. Though opposing armies suffered heavy losses, neither made any significant territorial gains. Typically, territorial animals become less aggressive towards their familiar neighbors. However, Argentine ants may not exhibit the “dear enemy effect,” which tends to quell these confrontations, according to IFL.Without the possibility of peace, encounters between rival colonies may continue to trigger violent confrontations. The researchers concluded that their findings were “inconsistent with a model of relaxed ecological constraints leading to colony fusion.” They also suggested that environmental cues were not the primary determinants of nestmate recognition in wild Argentine ant populations.The future of California ant colonies remains uncertain.IFL concludes that academic research has not extensively revisited the San Diego territorial wars in about two decades, leaving it unclear whether the boundaries have shifted or the fighting continues.

title: Atomic-6 space armor makes orbital debut after hypervelocity impact trials
content: Atomic-6 has announced that its proprietary Space Armor technology has been deployed into space for the first time. Installed on a Portal Space Systems’ Starburst-1 spacecraft, the craft was launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 during its Bandwagon-5 launch from Cape Canaveral, Florida.Atomic-6’s Space Armor is a new lightweight composite armor for satellites designed to help them survive impacts from space debris. Specifically, it is designed to absorb impacts from tiny impactors without creating more debris of its own.You can liken it to a kind of bulletproof vest for spacecraft. And the need for this kind of protection is only growing.Currently, the space around our planet is full of junk. Not just dead satellites and discarded rocket stages, but millions of tiny fragments travelling at enormous relative velocities.Even a tiny fragment can cause catastrophic damage when it hits a satellite at these kinds of velocities. Consider a 3 mm diameter aluminum sphere travelling at 7 km/s (15,659 mph/25,200 kph). Space debris armor for satellitesIf the debris only weighed about 38 milligrams, it could deliver something like 0.93 kilojoules of kinetic energy on impact. That’s roughly comparable to the muzzle energy of some powerful handgun rounds, although the physics of a hypervelocity impact are very different.And, just like a bullet, the energy is concentrated into a relatively small impact area. Such small pieces of junk are also impossible to track and therefore avoid. One solution is to simply clad your spacecraft in armor to take the hit. Various solutions exist today, but one of the most common is something called a Whipple Shield.Such armor typically consists of an outer sacrificial bumper that is separated from the main craft by space. When hit, the projectile breaks up, melts, and partially vaporizes. The resulting cloud of fragments spreads the impact over a much larger area, allowing the rear wall to withstand it more effectively. Another rear wall attached to the craft then safely absorbs this cloud of debris.While effective, this armor can produce more debris of its own, turning a single piece of junk into even more. Such armor also increases the size of a spacecraft and can be bulky.This is where Atomic-6’s armor comes into its own. Its solution is to provide a means of protecting the craft while also preventing the generation of even more junk. Proof of the pudding is in the eatingIt is also designed to be lightweight and relatively thin. The exact composition of its armour tiles is proprietary, but the company describes using a specialised fibre-to-resin manufacturing process. That suggests a carefully engineered composite in which reinforcing fibres are embedded in a polymer matrix.The result is a relatively light material able to prevent penetration while also absorbing secondary debris. It is also described as radio-frequency transparent, meaning it can be applied not only to the main “hull” but also to antennae and other comms equipment. While Space Armor has already undergone ground-based hypervelocity testing, its deployment aboard Starburst-1 offers an opportunity to assess its performance in orbit. Atomic-6 is actually hoping the spacecraft gets struck by debris, allowing the company to capture the impact on camera and assess the shield’s performance using onboard telemetry“We’ve proven Space Armor® tiles can withstand debris traveling at extraordinary speeds without generating harmful secondary fragments,” Trevor Smith, CEO, Atomic-6, told PR Newswire. “Now, we’re putting that technology to work aboard Portal’s Starburst-1, taking an important step toward scaling its deployment and making space safer and more sustainable,” he added.

title: Four-legged robot solves giant Rubik's Cube without using hands
content: ETH Zurich’s Robotic Systems Lab has showcased its ANYmal-D solving a giant Rubik’s Cube entirely on its own. While not unprecedented for a robot, what makes this feat interesting is that the robot achieved this using its legs while maintaining balance.Technically called pedipulation (manipulating objects with feet), the team managed this using a combination of classical algorithms, computer vision, and reinforcement learning. Solving a Rubik’s Cube requires several separate tasks. The first is to understand the starting state of the cube by examining all six faces to see which colors are where.The next is to plan how to solve it mathematically or, in other words, you need to figure out the sequence of rotations needed. Depending on your knowledge level, this can include executing basic “algorithms” to run through the classic “white cross,” “white corners”, “middle layer,” “yellow cross,” etc or faster methods.But all stages require physical manipulation of the cube to complete each move. Especially in a way that doesn’t accidentally move the wrong pieces. Solving a Rubik’s Cube with legsFor humans, this is usually the easiest part of the process, but for something like a four-legged robot it can be extremely challenging. Since it lacks hands, it needs to move layers and flip the entire cube, all using its legs while maintaining its balance.To achieve this, ANYmal had to balance on its remaining legs, precisely position its feet, apply the correct forces, and continuously adjust for what happens when it touches the cube. For this particular enterprise, the cube itself weighed in at around 10 pounds (4.6 kg).To successfully complete just one move, the robot needs to ensure the bottom layer doesn’t move, while also applying enough torque to move the desired layer. And, critically, it must do this repeatedly and not fall over.One accidental move could ruin the attempt, requiring a correction at best, and a possible restart at worst. According to the team, this was achieved through a combination of reinforcement learning, simulation, and “teacher–student training.”So, instead of hard-coding instructions for its limbs, the robot was able to learn “muscle memory” through trial and error. But that is only part of the challenge; just moving the cube around won’t necessarily solve it.For this part, the team gave the robot something called Kociemba’s solver to figure out what moves are needed. A combination of computer vision, color classification, and the algorithm is then used to work out the sequence.Potential industrial applicationsThis was then used to tell the robot’s limbs what moves to make, all the while monitoring the cube’s state to check and correct for errors. And the result? According to the team, the robot was able to solve 3 out of 3 attempted solves. Each solve took between 8 and 9 minutes to complete, requiring about 30 separate robotic actions.Not bad, especially for a robot that has no hands. But what, if any, are the wider implications for this research?Well, it shows that robots can be taught to use tools they already have in more unconventional ways to solve problems.It could, for example, enable a robot to open doors, manipulate valves, move obstructions, etc., using its legs instead of requiring specialist tools to be installed. That could translate into simpler, lighter, and potentially cheaper robots in the future.That could eventually be valuable in industrial inspection, maintenance, search and rescue, and other environments where a robot needs to do more than move around.

title: A cosmic ‘dragon egg’ may reveal how universe’s biggest stars begin
content: A possible massive-star embryo has an intriguing combination of features that includes an exceptionally compact center, a vast surrounding reservoir of cold gas and dust, and no convincing signs of energetic outflows. Nicknamed the ‘dragon egg,’ this object could offer a rare look at how massive stars begin forming. The researchers describe it as “a promising compact high-mass core candidate” in their study.However, astronomers still cannot tell how much mass is concentrated in its tiny core—or whether a protostar has already formed. This makes the object particularly interesting because scientists still debate how stars with at least eight times the Sun’s mass take shape.One theory proposes that a massive core assembles first and collapses into a star. Another suggests that a smaller seed grows by drawing in material from the surrounding cloud. By revealing the structure of a possible early-stage object, the dragon egg could help researchers investigate these competing ideas.ALMA reveals a compact centerThe dragon egg, designated C2c1a, lies in an infrared-dark cloud called Dragon Cloud, about 16,300 light-years from Earth. Its parent clump contains around 1,061 solar masses but emits little energy relative to its mass, a sign that it may be at an early stage of massive-star formation.Earlier observations suggested that C2c1a contained 20 to 30 solar masses, but they could not establish how tightly that mass was concentrated or whether a protostar had formed. To investigate, a team led by Ashley Thomas Barnes of the European Southern Observatory used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) to observe the region at a wavelength of 1.3 millimeters.The new observations resolved six components: the brightest source, C2c1a(a), another prominent component, C2c1b, and four fainter structures. Unlike the surrounding region, C2c1a(a) remained a single compact source, with an estimated radius of about 87 astronomical units (AU). One AU is the average distance between Earth and the Sun. No smaller fragments were detected within it at the observations’ resolution limit of roughly 175 AU. “The region resolves into multiple fragments, but the brightest component, C2c1a(a), remains a single compact continuum peak down to ∼ 175 au,” the study authors added.The compact source had a brightness temperature of about 40 kelvin, compared with a gas temperature of roughly 10 kelvin inferred from earlier observations. This difference points to a strong temperature gradient, with a warmer inner region embedded in colder material.Yet the compact source sits inside a much larger reservoir containing about 110 solar masses of gas and dust across scales of roughly 10,000 AU. Some of this material could eventually feed the developing object, although the observations do not establish how much will do so.The missing signs of a young starThe researchers searched for emissions from hot gas that might indicate a developing star, as well as outflows—streams of material often driven away from young stars. They found no strong signals of hot gas at the center and no convincing high-velocity outflow associated with the compact source.“A weak, deeply embedded, or unfavorably oriented outflow cannot be excluded, but the present data reveal no clear outflow signature from the compact source,” the study authors said.Some faint molecular emissions were present, but they were spread across the region rather than concentrated at the center. The source could be cold, or thick dust could be obscuring warmer material inside. The absence of a clear outflow also does not rule out a young star: a weak, deeply embedded or unfavorably oriented outflow could escape detection.The core’s mass remains uncertain, too. Depending on assumptions about the dust temperature and how it emits radiation, estimates range from roughly two to 30 solar masses. It could be a massive, cold core or a warmer, less massive object surrounded by a much larger reservoir.A promising clue, not a verdictThe compact structure and lack of clear stellar activity are consistent with models of star formation in which a massive core forms before collapsing into a star. However, the observations cannot rule out a smaller seed that grows by gathering material from its surroundings.More detailed measurements of the dust temperature, internal structure and gas motions are needed to determine what the dragon egg contains. For now, ALMA has exposed a remarkably compact source inside a massive cold reservoir—but the crucial question of how its central object will grow remains unanswered.The study is published in the journal arXiv.

title: US to expand space-based hardware production with new facility
content:
“The support we received from the Weld County Commissioners and the State of Colorado played a key role in our ability to locate this essential production work for the company in Colorado, extending our manufacturing presence in the state.”
Facility will enhance BAE Systems’ manufacturing capabilities
The facility, located on approximately 13 acres, will enhance the company’s manufacturing capabilities to meet customer demand and business growth related to space-based hardware and sensor
“Weld County is excited to welcome and partner with BAE Systems as they establish a new production facility in Northern Colorado,” said Scott James, Chair of the Weld County Board of Commissioners.
“Projects of this scale are transformational, not only because of the capital investment and high-quality employment they bring, but because they strengthen the entire industry ecosystem and create new opportunities for businesses, workers, and families across the region. This industry provides skilled high-paying jobs for both factory workers and engineers, and this represents a strong opportunity for economic growth and diversification.”
The company revealed that it will hire more than 200 new employees to support production at the new Weld County
facility
over the next 12 to 24 months. At full capacity, the company estimates that the new facility could feature approximately 600 employees.
BAE Systems plans to begin the retrofit process of the facility and procuring equipment throughout the rest of the year and anticipates opening the facility for production in early 2028, according to a press release.
“Colorado continues to lead the nation in aerospace and advanced manufacturing, and we are thrilled to welcome BAE Systems’ expansion in Weld County,” said Colorado Gov. Jared Polis. “This investment will bring hundreds of good-paying jobs to Weld County and further solidify our state as a hub for cutting-edge technology and innovation.”
The expansion is designed to meet growing demand for space-based hardware and sensor technologies, which are important components of modern aerospace, defense and space missions. By increasing its manufacturing capacity, the company aims to strengthen its ability to deliver advanced systems to customers.
With facility upgrades and equipment procurement planned before production begins, BAE Systems is preparing for a phased expansion at the Weld County site. The anticipated early 2028 production start will mark the next stage of the company’s investment in Colorado.
The project also reflects the increasing importance of reliable manufacturing capacity in industries that depend on sophisticated electronic, sensing and space-related technologies.
The Weld County facility will complement BAE Systems’ existing production operations in Boulder, Broomfield and Westminster. The additional site will further strengthen the company’s manufacturing network in Colorado and provide additional capacity for its growing space and sensor systems business.

title: Scientists uncover how insect-killing bacteria could lead to antibiotics
content: A new study examined bacteria that live in tiny worms that kill insects, and it could help develop new antibiotics. Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology and the University of Marburg studied how these bacteria produce different versions of GameXPeptides, which kill insects.The study, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, investigated how these bacterial compounds evolved, as changes in the bacteria’s DNA over time altered the GameXPeptides. This diversity could lead to new medicines, as these peptides belong to a broader class called nonribosomal peptides. How bacteria develop different chemical weaponsAccording to the study, researchers examined GameXPeptides in Xenorhabdus and Photorhabdus bacteria that live with tiny worms called nematodes. When nematodes enter an insect host, the bacteria are released and produce these compounds that kill it.The team reconstructed the evolutionary history of GxpS, the enzyme that produces GameXPeptides, to investigate how different peptide structures evolved. The study identified 49 compounds, including side products. “It felt like playing five-dimensional chess,” said Georg Hochberg, a researcher at the University of Marburg, in Phys.“Frequent recombination obscures the evolutionary history of these enzymes—each recombination event overwrites a piece of their past. But it is precisely this complexity that makes the system so fascinating.”The study continued that natural selection, genetic drift, and recombination biases shape the evolution of nonribosomal peptides, a class of compounds used in antibiotics such as penicillin, as well as toxins.“If we better understand the mechanisms underlying bacterial natural product diversity, it may become possible to discover new antibiotics that overcome existing resistances,” as stated in the study. Scientists found three forces that help to explain why different versions of GameXPeptide exist. Understanding these processes could help scientists discover other versions of other nonribosomal peptides. But natural selection alone does not account for the diversity of these compounds. Random mutations and genetic exchange also shape which variants emerge. When DNA is exchanged or rearranged, it creates new genetic combinations, a process called recombination. The researchers identified 27 synonymous recombination events that did not alter peptide structures and 26 nonsynonymous events that could change them. The team also found that recombination was more likely between enzyme domains with similar DNA sequences, particularly within the same gene. This bias limited which peptide variants could emerge through recombination.Findings could inform future antibiotic researchThe study examined one family of peptide-producing enzymes. The researchers said further work would be needed to determine whether the same evolutionary principles apply to peptides that humans use in medicine.However, that being said, many antibiotics are nonribosomal peptides. These researchers might have opened up an avenue to explore that might allow scientists to investigate new antibiotics.“Our results show that the conceptual framework we developed for the GameXPeptides can serve as a guide to decipher the evolutionary forces acting on other natural product families, such as the polyketide synthases, which like NRPS, produce many clinically relevant natural products,” Helge Bode of the Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology said in Phys. By understanding how these products evolve and diversify in bacteria, scientists might be able to tackle current resistance that humans have developed to some of the antibiotics that exist.

title: China explores wing-mounted radar to expand airborne surveillance
content: Chinese military aircraft designers have proposed a new airborne early-warning radar that would fit inside an aircraft’s wing rather than a conventional nose-mounted radome or large radar dome above the fuselage. The concept uses changes in flight attitude and coordination between multiple unmanned aircraft to expand surveillance coverage, potentially giving smaller platforms some of the capabilities traditionally associated with dedicated early-warning aircraft.The design was outlined in a study published in the Chinese peer-reviewed journal Measurement & Control Technology. Its authors include Ren Yunsong and researchers affiliated with the AVIC Chengdu Aircraft Design and Research Institute, which developed China’s J-20 stealth fighter and designed the two-seat J-20S variant intended to operate alongside unmanned aircraft.A radar array built into the wingConventional fighter aircraft typically house their primary radar in the nose, behind a protective radome. Meanwhile, airborne early-warning aircraft often use large radar arrays mounted above the fuselage to provide surveillance over a broad area. Both approaches have limitations: fighter noses restrict the size of the antenna, while large radar structures add weight, drag and complexity.The Chinese team proposes embedding the radar antenna, control components and associated equipment inside the aircraft’s wing. The antenna’s radiating surface would face downward, with a protective cover following the wing’s external contours. This arrangement could provide a larger antenna aperture without requiring a prominent external radar dome, the South China Morning Post reported.The main challenge is that wings offer considerable surface area but have relatively thin cross-sections, limiting the volume available for radar hardware. The design therefore seeks to use the wing’s surface more efficiently while relying on aircraft manoeuvres to steer the radar’s coverage.In one proposed operating mode, an unmanned aircraft would roll more than 45 degrees, tilting the wing-mounted antenna toward the side of the aircraft. By changing its flight attitude, the platform could redirect the radar beam toward different sectors without depending entirely on a mechanically rotating antenna.Multiple aircraft could work as a distributed radar networkThe proposal is based on distributed air combat, a concept explored by DARPA in 2014. Rather than depending on a single, expensive aircraft to provide broad-area surveillance, distributed operations would use multiple smaller platforms to share detection and tracking responsibilities.The researchers describe four operating modes for the wing-mounted radar, covering all-direction and multi-direction detection, wide-area surveillance, concentrated searches for specific targets and coordinated operations designed to counter electronic interference. Several aircraft could divide surveillance tasks or combine their efforts to improve coverage in a particular sector.This approach could help address a central challenge in airborne early warning, which is providing extensive detection coverage without relying on a small number of large, expensive platforms. Conventional early-warning aircraft have space for substantial radar arrays and powerful onboard systems, but their size and cost can limit how many can be deployed. Thus, smaller unmanned aircraft could potentially offer greater flexibility if they can achieve sufficient detection performance and coordinate reliably.The concept could eventually be considered for future Chinese combat aircraft, including the J-20 and next-gen designs commonly referred to as the J-36 and J-50. However, the paper does not identify any of these aircraft as a confirmed platform for the technology, nor does it disclose a development schedule or flight-test results.

title: Container-based system launches missiles, can be deployed on ships
content: A Norwegian defense technology company has successfully showcased a containerized misile launch system. Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace demonstrated that the flexible deployment concept could expand the missile’s operational use across land-based positions, mobile vehicles, and naval platforms.Known as the NSM Mission Module, the system packages up to four missile canisters inside a standard 20-foot shipping container, offering a potentially simpler way to deploy precision anti-ship strike capabilities.Missile was launched from container-based unitThe test was conducted in Norway, where the missile was launched from a container-based unit holding up to four missiles. The objective was to verify safety aspects, logistical parameters related to handling and loading, as well as the system’s ability to manage pressure and blast effects during launch. The prototype underwent testing at an undisclosed military range in Norway in early October 2026. The company-funded demonstration was intended to validate the concept, reduce integration risks, and help prospective customers assess the feasibility of adopting a containerized missile-launching solution.The development reflects a broader shift in modern defense planning towards modular weapons systems that can be transported, repositioned, and integrated into different operational environments with fewer platform-specific modifications.Containerized solution represents an alternative way of deploying missile capabilityThe containerized solution represents an alternative way of deploying missile capability. By integrating the launcher into a standard shipping container, the solution can be transported more easily, moved between locations, and incorporated into existing logistics and transportation networks. A launching container can be deployed, without modifications, from ships, trucks or directly from the ground. “A containerized solution can be pre-positioned and deployed discreetly to support operations wherever the need arises. At the same time, it enables capabilities to be distributed across larger areas, providing greater operational flexibility and more deployment options,” said Ståle Mortensson, Vice President BD & Strategy in Missiles & Aerostructures. “There is growing interest in concepts that enable capabilities to be distributed and repositioned across large geographic areas, with a containerized solution representing one possible approach.”Naval Strike Missiles mounted on launcher mechanismThe NSM Mission Module is designed around a conventional 20-foot International Organization for Standardization (ISO) shipping container. Inside, the system accommodates four canisterized Naval Strike Missiles mounted on an elevating launcher mechanism.The container’s roof opens before launch, allowing the internal launcher to rise into its firing position. Following launch, the mechanism can retract into the container, preserving the system’s compact configuration for transportation and storage.Kongsberg has also integrated supporting equipment into the container, including a generator, an electronics compartment, and the mechanisms required to manage launch-related blast effects. Mission planning remains an external function.This arrangement is significant because it brings several essential launcher components together within a transportable module. Rather than requiring every host platform to accommodate a permanently installed, purpose-built launcher, operators could potentially employ the container as a mission-specific payload, subject to the necessary integration, safety, and operational requirements.

title: 220-ton cranes help raise a 928-foot bridge tower in China’s mountains
content: Chinese construction equipment manufacturer Zoomlion has supplied two heavy-duty tower cranes for the construction of the Lugu Lake Grand Bridge in southwestern China, helping crews complete a 283-meter main tower on the Shangri-La side of the crossing.The tower reached its topping-out milestone on September 29, according to Zoomlion. The bridge is part of the Xichang–Shangri-La Expressway, where construction across mountainous terrain requires precise lifting and positioning of large structural components.The project used two of Zoomlion’s R4300-200 tower cranes, one serving each of the bridge’s main towers. The equipment is designed for heavy lifting at height, combining high load capacity with automated safety systems and remote operation capabilities.Cranes lift 200-ton loads at mountain bridge siteThe R4300-200 has a maximum lifting capacity of 200 metric tons (220 US tons) and an 80-meter jib (262 feet). Zoomlion says the crane incorporates more than 20 intelligent safety and control functions, including collision prevention, automatic operating-speed adjustments based on load, and mechanisms designed to prevent suspended loads from slipping downward.These capabilities were particularly relevant during the final 103 meters (338 feet) of construction on the Shangri-La side tower. Crews had to position the final steel and concrete sections above the central crossbeam, where changing wind conditions added to the challenges of maintaining load stability and alignment.Live camera feeds allowed operators to monitor lifting operations and control the cranes remotely from ground level. This arrangement provided visibility of component positioning while allowing operators to make precise adjustments during installation.Zoomlion said the segment-lifting work on the tower was completed safely. The announcement did not specify the bridge’s full length or when the entire crossing is expected to open.Customized cranes support Istanbul skyscraperThe bridge project follows Zoomlion’s work on the 380-meter (1,247 feet) tower housing the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye at the Istanbul International Financial Center.Unlike the bridge tower, the Istanbul project involved a high-rise building that combined steel framing and precast concrete on a constrained urban construction site. According to Zoomlion, the project required 1,260 heavy lifts, including steel columns weighing up to 48.2 metric tons (53.1 US tons).To meet those requirements, the company customized its L760-50 luffing-jib tower crane, which has a maximum lifting capacity of 50 metric tons (55 US tons) and a maximum jib length of 60 meters (197 feet).Its modular mast sections measure 2.3 meters (7.5 feet) on each side, allowing them to be transported in standard shipping containers. Each crane also required 10 custom connections to the building, engineered to meet local seismic requirements.Variable-frequency drives regulate lifting, rotation, and jib movement, enabling smoother starts and stops and finer adjustments when positioning heavy components. Wind-speed monitoring provides warnings and reduces operating speeds when preset thresholds are exceeded.Remote monitoring helps manage maintenanceZoomlion also used remote monitoring technology to track equipment performance during the Istanbul project. The system transmitted 28 operating parameters, including load data, component temperatures, operating hours, and fault codes.These measurements helped teams assess equipment wear and plan preventive maintenance. Zoomlion’s research and development team in China worked remotely with engineers in Türkiye to diagnose issues and support maintenance, aiming to limit downtime.The company says its equipment selection and technical support helped sustain a construction pace of one floor every five days for the main structure. Support also covered crane placement, installation feasibility studies and dismantling simulations.Applying heavy-lifting experience to new projectsZoomlion says experience from the bridge and Istanbul projects is informing its work on other high-rise developments, including the 377-meter (1,237 feet) Ciel Dubai Marina hotel, Dubai’s 400-meter (1,312 feet) Al Habtoor Tower and Indonesia’s 331-meter (1,086 feet) Oasis Central Towers.The projects show different demands on tower-crane engineering. Bridge construction requires accurate placement of structural sections across exposed sites, while skyscraper construction can demand compact equipment configurations, custom building connections, and continuous coordination as structures rise.In both cases, crane capacity is only one part of the challenge. Control systems, wind monitoring, installation planning and maintenance support also affect how safely and efficiently heavy components can be positioned at height.

title: US drinking water may contain 2x reported levels of 'forever chemicals’
content: The methods used to report harmful “forever chemicals” in U.S. drinking water may be underestimating their concentrations by more than half, according to a study published in Cell Reports Sustainability.Researchers analyzed more than 1.8 million measurement records from across the United States. They found that conventional calculations captured only 44.1 percent of the modeled concentration of perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in community water systems.The findings suggest current methods may be understating the amount of PFAS present in water. PFAS, or per and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are called “forever chemicals” because they do not degrade naturally, and man-made processes to destroy them are costly and yield questionable results.Most PFAS measurements fall below reporting limitsUnder the Environmental Protection Agency’s fifth Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR 5), public water systems monitor 29 PFAS in drinking water. The researchers examined 1,863,306 PFAS measurement records from 10,297 monitored systems across the country, “of which 2 percent were detections above the reporting limit.”“Replacing these non-detects with zero, half the detection limit, or the detection limit itself remains a common practice in water-quality monitoring,” researchers wrote, adding that these methods can introduce biases into estimated averages and other statistical measurements.Results below reporting limits do not necessarily indicate the absence of PFAS. They represent concentrations that laboratories cannot quantify with current methods.Models reveal substantially higher PFAS estimatesTo investigate the missing concentrations, the researchers developed a statistical framework that accounts for results below laboratory reporting limits.The team generated 500 model estimates and calculated average concentrations for 25 PFAS detected at least once in the national dataset. For those chemicals, the model estimated a population-weighted average concentration of 15.04 nanograms per liter (parts per trillion), compared with 6.63 nanograms per liter when below-limit results were counted as zero. The conventional calculation fell 55.9 percent short of the model’s estimate.For the six PFAS included in the EPA’s April 2024 National Primary Drinking Water Regulation, the conventional calculation produced an average of 2.62 nanograms per liter, compared with the model’s estimate of 5.23 nanograms per liter.“Across sensitivity analyses, the direction of the national finding was consistent, but its magnitude was model dependent,” according to the study.Findings could improve future water monitoringDespite the notable differences, the researchers emphasized that their models do not directly measure unknown PFAS concentrations or establish additional health risks.“Our study only examines how PFAS measurements are summarized,” lead author Gehendra Kharel told Phys.org. “It does not establish that every below-limit result poses a health risk.”The researchers also examined whether lowering laboratory reporting limits could reduce the gap between conventional calculations and model estimates.For PFOA and PFOS, two widely studied PFAS, models indicated that reducing reporting limits from 4 nanograms per liter to 0.5 nanograms per liter would allow conventional calculations to capture more than 92 percent of modeled occurrence, according to the study.The authors concluded that improved laboratory sensitivity and statistical methods could help agencies better interpret drinking-water monitoring results.“When a water quality report says ‘not detected,’ that means below the reporting limit, not zero,” added Kharel.“Our method gives water agencies and utilities a way to account for that difference, so they can see where more testing would help and be clearer about what they do and do not know.”

title: This Chinese crossover drove 742 miles on one charge and one tank
content: China’s XPeng has demonstrated the long-distance capability of its Mona L05 extended-range electric vehicle (EREV), with the crossover covering 1,194.2 km (742 miles) without recharging or refueling during a road test. The result represents 94.77 percent of its claimed combined range under China’s CLTC testing standard.XPeng shared footage of the test on October 23, following a drive organized by Chinese automotive platform BitAuto, also known as Yiche. The vehicle traveled from Guangzhou to Wenzhou along the G228 coastal highway, completing the journey in 23 hours and 14 minutes.The test was conducted in “Ultra Power Saving Mode,” which disabled most nonessential vehicle functions to reduce energy consumption. The climate control was set to 24°C (75°F). XPeng did not disclose the average speed, although footage reportedly showed the vehicle traveling at around 50–80 km/h (31-50 mph) for much of the journey.How the extended-range powertrain worksThe Mona L05 EREV combines a 183-kilowatt (245-horsepower) electric motor with a 37.2-kilowatt-hour lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated gasoline engine.Unlike a conventional hybrid, an extended-range electric vehicle primarily uses an electric motor to drive its wheels. Its combustion engine serves as a range extender, generating electricity when the battery can no longer provide all the energy required for driving.According to Car News China, during the test, the Mona L05 initially traveled 252.7 km (157 miles) using battery power alone, recording electricity consumption of 11.7 kWh per 100 km (18.8 kWh per 100 miles). The range-extender engine then activated to support the remainder of the journey.XPeng lists a maximum electric-only range of 310 km (193 miles) and a combined CLTC range of up to 1,310 km (814 miles) for the EREV version. The road test therefore covered nearly 95 percent of its advertised combined range without an intermediate stop to replenish either energy source.Over the full journey, the reported electricity consumption was 2.5 kWh per 100 km (4.0 kWh per 100 miles), and gasoline consumption was 3.7 liters per 100 km (approximately 63.6 US mpg). These figures reflect the particular test conditions rather than a guarantee of everyday efficiency.A long-range alternative to battery-only EVsThe Mona L05 is also available as a fully battery-electric vehicle. That version uses a larger 71.1-kWh LFP battery and the same 183-kW electric motor, with a claimed CLTC range of 615–660 km (382–410 miles), depending on configuration.The two versions address different driving needs. The battery-electric model offers a longer electric-only range, while the EREV adds a gasoline-powered electricity source for longer journeys where charging opportunities may be limited.The vehicle measures 4,870 mm (191.7 inches) long, 1,930 mm (76.0 inches) wide and 1,636 mm (64.4 inches) tall, with a 2,940-mm (115.7-inch) wheelbase. Its listed features include a 17.3-inch central touchscreen, a 26.8-inch head-up display and a 702-liter (24.8-cubic-foot) trunk.The Mona L05 was offered for presale in China at 169,800–191,800 yuan, equivalent to approximately $25,400–$28,700 at the exchange rates cited in reports. These are Chinese-market prices, and the range-test announcement has not established availability in other markets.What the test does and does not showThe 1,194-km (742-mile) run offers a useful indication of the Mona L05 EREV’s long-distance capability under a specific set of conditions. However, the energy-saving mode, relatively moderate speeds, and limited disclosure of the test methodology make it difficult to compare the result directly with everyday driving.Higher highway speeds, heavier loads, weather conditions and frequent acceleration can all affect real-world range and fuel consumption. The result should therefore be viewed as a reported road-test achievement rather than a universal estimate of how far every driver can travel.Still, the test highlights the appeal of extended-range electric vehicles: they can deliver substantial battery-powered driving while retaining a combustion-engine-based option for journeys that exceed the battery’s standalone range.

title: Sodium-ion batteries promise 20% lower costs for grid energy storage
content: General Motors is backing a sodium-ion battery push aimed at making electricity storage cheaper for utilities and data centers.Peak Energy, a sodium-ion battery startup backed by General Motors through its investment arm GM Ventures, announced on October 23 that it had raised $108 million in an oversubscribed Series B funding round.GM Ventures led the round, with participation from LG Technology Ventures and other investors, to support the company’s expansion into grid and data center energy storage.The startup plans to expand manufacturing, fulfill more than $1 billion in existing customer orders, and bring its passively cooled battery storage systems to the data center market. Its platform eliminates active cooling equipment, which the company says can reduce storage costs and energy waste.The funding builds on a partnership announced June 10. GM will develop next-generation sodium-ion cells at its Michigan battery laboratories and retain exclusive manufacturing rights, while Peak Energy will integrate the cells into its stationary storage systems.A battery built for the gridThe partnership focuses on grid storage rather than electric vehicles. Stationary batteries have different requirements from vehicle batteries, making cost, reliability, and safety more important than packing maximum energy into a small, lightweight package.Lithium-iron phosphate, or LFP, batteries currently dominate stationary storage. Peak Energy is pursuing sodium-ion as an alternative that uses more abundant, potentially lower-cost materials.GM’s vice president of battery and sustainability, Kurt Kelty, said the chemistry suits the application.“At GM, we know that the application should determine the battery, and for grid-scale stationary storage, sodium-ion is the right solution,” Kelty said.“Peak is already demonstrating the value of sodium-ion through their innovative energy storage platform, and together we’re working to push those benefits even further with our next-generation cell – helping deliver more reliable, lower-cost energy storage at scale for the US grid,” he added.Removing active cooling equipmentPeak Energy’s approach extends beyond battery chemistry to the equipment surrounding the cells.Conventional LFP storage systems use active cooling to manage operating temperatures. That equipment adds components, consumes electricity, and increases system complexity.The company says its sodium-ion platform operates with passive cooling, eliminating the need for those systems.According to the company, the platform can lower energy storage costs by 20 percent compared with conventional systems while delivering more than 99 percent uptime. These figures are company-reported and have not been independently verified.Peak Energy also estimates that replacing conventional LFP storage with its technology could reduce annual battery-storage energy waste across the US by up to two terawatt-hours.That projection concerns potential savings from broader deployment, rather than energy already saved by installed systems.Manufacturing for rising electricity demandThe new funding will support Peak’s manufacturing expansion as utilities add storage alongside renewable generation and electricity demand grows.Data centers represent another target, particularly as AI infrastructure increases power demand. Peak Energy plans to bring its passively cooled storage platform to that market while working through its existing customer orders.

title: Slow-moving light helps silicon chip hit 200 Gb/s for AI data centers
content: AI data centers need to move enormous amounts of data between chips, but making those connections faster without increasing energy consumption remains a challenge. Researchers in Japan have developed a compact silicon optical modulator that transmits data at up to 200 gigabits per second (Gb/s), using slow-moving light and a built-in electrical equalizer to overcome a speed limitation that has hindered similar devices.Conventional silicon modulators, which convert electrical signals into light, typically measure several millimeters and face a trade-off between efficient modulation and high-frequency performance. Slowing light strengthens its interaction with a device, improving efficiency, but electrical resistance can limit how quickly the modulator responds. The new design addresses both problems, potentially helping data centers accommodate more optical connections while reducing energy consumption. “We created a silicon photonic crystal waveguide optical modulator that integrates a built-in electro-optic equalizer to break the bandwidth limitation while preserving the benefits of the slow-light effect,” Toshihiko Baba, one of the study authors and a professor at YOKOHAMA National University, said.The power of slow light and an equalizerThe researchers combined two techniques in a single silicon device. Its photonic crystal waveguide (a tiny structure that guides light through a silicon chip) contains a carefully arranged pattern of tiny holes that controls how light travels through the material, allowing it to propagate more slowly than in an ordinary waveguide.This slow-light effect strengthens the interaction between light and the device, allowing a small electrical change to produce a larger change in the outgoing light signal. The result is more efficient modulation in a smaller space.Conventional slow-light modulators, however, face a problem. Electrical resistance limits their high-frequency response, restricting how quickly they can process changing signals.To overcome this limitation, the researchers added a built-in electro-optic (EO) equalizer that helps the modulator handle faster-changing signals. It adjusts how different parts of the light signal combine, allowing the device to maintain its performance at higher speeds. As a result, the range of signal frequencies the device could handle increased from 35 to 80 gigahertz (GHz) in one design and from 23 to 55 GHz in another.Achieving incredible data transmission speedThe researcher fabricated the device using a 300-millimeter silicon-on-insulator manufacturing process. The complete device measures just 320 micrometers (µm) in length, including its main and equalizer sections, compared with 2–4 millimeters for conventional silicon Mach-Zehnder modulators. The entire device, including its electrodes, occupies approximately 0.4 square millimeters. With a low-complexity 11-tap equalizer at the receiver, the team achieved 140 Gb/s using on-off keying, in which light represents data through two signal levels. The modulator consumed 26 femtojoules (fJ) per bit, a femtojoule is an extremely small unit of energy which is equal to one quadrillionth of a joule..Using pulse-amplitude modulation with four signal levels (PAM-4), the researchers achieved 180 Gb/s without digital signal processing (DSP). Adding the 11-tap receiver equalizer increased the rate to 200 Gb/s, with the modulator consuming 63 fJ per bit.The best part is, “slow light can be fabricated using CMOS-compatible processes, simultaneously satisfying high speed, low power consumption and small footprint requirements, meeting the next-generation optical transmitter needs of AI data centers,” Baba added.This means for this approach, there is no need for specialized manufacturing steps often required by some alternative materials, such as thin-film lithium niobate.A smaller modulator still has hurdles to clearThe design could help data centers accommodate denser optical connections while limiting energy use. However, its optical insertion loss — the reduction in light intensity as it passes through a device — remains relatively high at 11.7–15.5 decibels. The researchers used an optical amplifier to compensate during their experiments, but practical applications would benefit from reducing this loss through design optimization.They also plan to expand the range of wavelengths the modulator can handle, potentially enabling multiple optical channels to operate together. The researchers estimate that integrating 16–32 channels could eventually support a combined capacity of 3.2–6.4 terabits per second. These figures are projections, not demonstrated results.“We believe that this architecture offers promise as a building block for future co-packaged optics in high-density data centers,” Baba said.The study is published in the journal Nature Communications.

title: AI-powered wearables recreate five food smells sent over the internet
content: The smell of coffee could become part of a virtual catch-up, thanks to an experimental system that connects odor sensors to wearable scent dispensers over the internet.Researchers at Ohio State University and Zhejiang Laboratory in China developed the automated system to identify smells using artificial intelligence and trigger their release near another person’s nose. Described in Science Advances, the technology combines chemical sensing, machine learning, and wearable devices shaped as bracelets or necklaces.In laboratory tests involving 14 healthy volunteers, participants identified individual odors with 73 percent accuracy and combinations with roughly 71 percent accuracy. The findings offer a step toward adding smell to digital experiences, although the system currently relies on preloaded scents.Turning chemical signals into digital instructionsRecreating smell presents a different challenge from reproducing images or sound. Cameras and microphones capture light and sound waves, while odors come from chemical compounds that must be detected and physically released for someone to experience them.Previous approaches have included bulky desktop equipment, scratch-and-sniff cards, and virtual reality headsets. Some also required a person at the receiving end to release a scent manually.The new system uses machine-learning algorithms to recognize patterns associated with volatile organic compounds, the molecules responsible for smells, and classify them into odor categories.That information travels over the internet to a receiving device called Scentronic, which releases the corresponding scent close to the user’s nose. The process sends digital instructions between devices; the odor itself comes from supplies already loaded into the wearable.Testing coffee, cake and mixed scentsThe researchers tested five odors: beer, cake, coffee, orange, and red wine. Volunteers encountered them individually and in combinations, including beer with cake and coffee with orange.Participants correctly identified individual smells 73 percent of the time. Recognition remained close to that level for combinations, reaching approximately 71 percent.Speed was another focus. The system responded to a scent signal in 0.6 seconds, although identifying more complex food odors required several seconds.The distinction matters because responding to a signal and accurately classifying an unfamiliar chemical mixture are separate tasks.The team also developed a version that dispenses scent-infused flavored liquids. This extends the concept beyond smelling an object remotely toward recreating aspects of a drinking experience.In a potential virtual reality application, a user could select a digital drink and receive a corresponding flavored liquid at home.Moving beyond controlled laboratory testsThe technology cannot yet reconstruct arbitrary smells from their basic chemical components. Instead, it selects from preloaded odor channels, limiting the range and precision of what it can reproduce.The researchers plan to test the system outside controlled laboratory conditions, introduce more complex evaluations, and improve controls for potential biases among participants.Possible applications include virtual social gatherings, online shopping, and healthcare research involving sensory perception or loss.For now, the work demonstrates a limited but automated connection between detecting an odor and recreating a corresponding scent elsewhere. Expanding that connection to the variety of smells people encounter daily remains the next challenge.

title: Suspected China rocket debris measuring 11-feet found in US cornfield
content: A farmer harvesting corn in west-central Minnesota discovered a scorched metal dome on October 14 that space observers suspect came from a Chinese rocket. Measuring about 11 feet, the object has raised questions about how the rocket returned to Earth.The bowl-shaped debris appears to be the end cap of a fuel tank and matches the diameter of LandSpace’s Zhuque-2E rocket, which launched on September 15.Its origin has not been confirmed, and LandSpace did not respond to a request for comment.British astronomer Jonathan McDowell, who has tracked launches for more than 30 years, believes the discovery points to a problem with the rocket’s descent. It could also open a diplomatic channel for compensation if the debris damaged the farmer’s property.A successful launch, followed by questionsThe Beijing-based company declared the September mission a success after the rocket deployed 10 satellites for the Qianfan internet network, a project similar to SpaceX‘s Starlink.The rocket subsequently restarted its engine as it began its return. Residents in Kansas and Minnesota posted videos of fiery debris crossing the sky shortly after the launch.McDowell suspects the engine fired slightly harder or longer than intended. Rather than entering a lower orbit and remaining there for several days before re-entry, the rocket stage may have descended immediately.That explanation remains his assessment, rather than a confirmed account of the mission. “It seems very unlikely that they would have targeted America,” he said.Why the dome may have survivedAn object this large surviving reentry is not necessarily unusual. Large, thin components, including fuel-tank end caps, can slow rapidly high in the atmosphere before heating enough to burn away.A previous example occurred in 1997, when a 250-kilogram steel fuel tank from a US Delta II rocket landed nearly intact in Texas.Rocket operators generally aim controlled reentries toward remote ocean areas to reduce the likelihood that surviving fragments will reach populated land.The Minnesota discovery also follows trouble on Zhuque-2E‘s previous flight in June, when its upper stage reportedly broke apart in orbit, creating dozens of fragments.“Restarting rocket engines in orbit is always hard,” said McDowell. “But it’s been done for a long time, and it’s meant to be a solved problem. Clearly, they’ve got some wrinkles to iron out,” he added.A possible claim between governmentsStevens County Sheriff Jason Dingman said he could not yet answer questions about the object, including its location, but expected further details to be released.If investigators establish its origin and identify property damage, the case could involve both Washington and Beijing.McDowell said the 1972 UN Space Liability Convention places responsibility for damage on the launching country. The farmer would therefore seek help from the US government, which could present a claim to China.No confirmed damage claim was described in the report, and identifying the object remains essential before assigning responsibility.For McDowell, the broader concern is repeated exposure to falling hardware as launches increase.
