title: A Single Enzyme Could Hold the Key to Treating a Devastating Brain Disorder
content:
Scientists have uncovered a surprising molecular chain reaction that may explain why Angelman syndrome disrupts brain development. Credit: Shutterstock
Blocking an enzyme’s production restored brain growth and healthy behaviors in mice engineered to develop Angelman syndrome, pointing to a possible treatment target.
Children with Angelman syndrome begin to show difficulties with thinking and movement at around 6 months of age. The rare condition occurs in approximately one in 20,000 births and is caused by the absence of a gene normally inherited from the mother. Researchers know which gene is missing, but they have struggled to explain why its absence causes these problems, making treatments elusive.
Research in mice now points to a chain of events that connects the missing gene to a stress response that interferes with brain growth. A team led by Jason Yi, PhD, an assistant professor of neuroscience at
Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis
, traced that response to a buildup of a normally harmless enzyme. The study was published in
One missing gene, many excess proteins
The missing gene,
, produces an enzyme called ubiquitin ligase, which helps keep cells orderly by marking unneeded proteins for disposal. It is active throughout the brain and participates in 60 different cellular processes. Identifying which of those processes contribute to Angelman syndrome required narrowing that broad field of possibilities.
Yi and his colleagues developed modified cells in the laboratory with
deactivated, then looked for proteins that accumulated without it. They identified 23 candidate proteins whose levels increased. One stood out for its strong connection to ubiquitin ligase’s normal housekeeping function: asparagine synthetase, an enzyme that helps cells produce essential proteins.
Researchers at WashU Medicine have shown in mice that slowed brain growth in Angelman’s syndrome is caused by elevated levels of a molecule called asparagine synthetase (green) in neurons (blue) that triggers the brain’s stress response. Credit: Jason Yi
A false alarm slows brain growth
In mice genetically modified to develop Angelman syndrome, elevated levels of asparagine synthetase activated the brain’s stress response. Yet the enzyme does not interact with the usual triggers for that response, and its overabundance does not otherwise damage the cell. The consequences instead arise indirectly, as the stress response sharply reduces protein production and growth.
“The neurons are tricked into thinking that they’re in stress when they’re not — that’s bad because they will then not grow normally,” Yi said, noting that most children with Angelman syndrome have smaller brains than their peers of the same age. “It’s a reaction from the brain trying to conserve resources to protect itself. It does suggest that there is a dysregulation in the brain we might be able to correct.”
An enzyme offers a possible treatment target
Blocking the production of asparagine synthetase restored normal brain growth and healthy behaviors in the mice. The team had corrected a later step in the biological sequence set off by the missing gene, allowing healthy development to resume.
The study is the first to link an increase in asparagine synthetase to a neurological condition. It adds to evidence that an imbalance in proteins can contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders by triggering stress responses, even when the proteins themselves are not directly damaging cells.
Yi said medications could potentially target the stress response triggered by asparagine synthetase, but much remains to be learned before work on a possible treatment can begin. His team is investigating precisely why the enzyme activates that response, where in the brain the response is most active, and when during development medical interventions would be most effective.
“We still don’t know a whole lot about the disease,” said Yi. “We haven’t been able to identify all of the things that the missing gene is doing and rescue the things that it is not doing in Angelman’s syndrome. But I think our data are the most complete so far to begin answering those questions.”
Reference: “Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes” by Kwang-Soo Kim, Cory Gardner, Alissa Cullen, Jalin A. Stelzer, Kevin Cho, Ashish Sharma, Mati T. Nemera, Travis Law, Huma Naz, Guoyan Zhao, Harrison W. Gabel, Gary J. Patti, Erik S. Musiek, Tae-Hyuk Ahn and Jason J. Yi, 21 October 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11165-4
Support for this work came from the Simons Foundation (Bridge to Independence award #387973), the Whitehall Foundation, the Hope Center for Neurological Disorders at Washington University (Pilot Award), and the National Institute of Mental Health (R01MH122786 and R01MH144153).

title: Just Two Days on a Vegan Diet Triggered Unexpected Changes in the Liver
content:
A new study in mice reveals how quickly the liver responds to changes in dietary protein, uncovering a crucial enzyme involved in maintaining metabolic balance. Credit: Shutterstock
Switching from a vegetarian to a vegan diet altered liver metabolism in mice within just two days, making glucose production and toxic waste removal less efficient.
Millions of people follow a vegan diet, excluding all animal-derived products. Plant-based eating is recommended in part for its environmental benefits, but the health consequences of getting all dietary protein from plants are not yet fully understood. For researchers, that raises a question about how the body responds when the source of its protein changes.
Scientists at the
University of Geneva (UNIGE)
investigated that question in mice, focusing on the liver, which helps maintain blood sugar and processes the components of dietary protein. Their study, published in
ar Metabolism
, compared a lacto-vegetarian diet containing both animal and plant proteins with a vegan diet.
“In just two days, the mice fed an exclusively vegan diet showed less efficient glucose production,” explains Pierre Maechler, full professor in the Department of Cell Physiology and Metabolism and at the Diabetes Center of the UNIGE Faculty of Medicine. “Furthermore, their livers were less effective at eliminating ammonia, a toxic substance released during the breakdown of amino acids. A significant reduction in physical activity also suggests effects on the body as a whole.”
Protein helps maintain blood sugar
Proteins from plants and animals consist of amino acids, small molecules joined together like links in a chain. Their types and proportions differ depending on the food source, so changing protein sources gives the body a different mixture to process. Plant proteins naturally contain fewer branched-chain amino acids than animal proteins. Along with helping build the body’s proteins, these amino acids supply some of the raw material the liver uses to produce glucose and maintain sufficient blood sugar during fasting.
“Overall, a change in diet alters liver metabolism very quickly, but this effect is just as rapidly reversible,” emphasizes Maechler. “The body adapts within one to two days to even subtle changes in dietary composition and returns to normal upon the reintroduction of animal proteins.”
Without GDH, ammonia builds up
The combination of less efficient glucose production and ammonia removal pointed the team toward a liver enzyme called glutamate dehydrogenase, or GDH. Located in mitochondria, the structures inside cells that help process fuel, GDH connects protein metabolism with sugar metabolism. To investigate its role, the researchers compared two groups of mice lacking the enzyme in their livers. One group ate a lacto-vegetarian diet, while the other ate a strict vegan diet.
Without GDH, the mice eating only plant proteins developed a severe buildup of ammonia and impaired blood glucose regulation compared with mice whose diet also included animal proteins. This confirmed the enzyme’s essential role in the metabolic response to an exclusively plant-based diet.
Human effects remain uncertain
The experiments were conducted in mice, so they do not establish that people would experience the same changes. They do, however, provide a way to investigate the physiological questions that accompany a change in protein source.
“In addition to the ethical and environmental considerations that often motivate a switch to a plant-based diet, there are also scientific factors relating to the physiological functioning of our metabolism that are worth being aware of,” notes Maechler.
For people following a strict vegan diet, the researchers emphasize choosing protein sources rich in branched-chain amino acids, such as nuts, tofu, and lentils, to support the liver’s metabolic functions. They place that consideration alongside the need to ensure an adequate intake of specific vitamins.
Reference: “Transition to dietary plant-based proteins requires functional liver GDH for proper control of ammonia and energy homeostasis” by Yan Zhou, Angela M. Ramos-Lobo, Tingting Fu, Hector Gallart-Ayala, Julijana Ivanisevic and Pierre Maechler, 4 September 2026,
Molecular Metabolism
DOI: 10.1016/j.molmet.2026.102435
The work was funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation (#310030_192486 to P.M.) and the canton of Geneva.

title: Earth’s Magnetic Shield Is Rippling Unevenly – Scientists Have Uncovered the Cause
content:
New computer simulations reveal an unexpected interaction between the solar wind and Earth’s magnetic shield. Credit: Stock
The solar wind can weaken the very waves it creates along Earth’s magnetic shield, simulations show, helping explain why some regions are more active than others.
Earth’s magnetic shield protects the planet, yet particles and energy from the Sun can still find their way through. Along its outer edge, a constant stream of solar material brushes past, stirring up waves where the two environments meet. A new study led by researchers at the University of Oulu explains why those waves grow stronger in some places than in others, revealing how uneven this boundary can be.
The protective region created by Earth’s magnetic field is called the magnetosphere, while the stream arriving from the Sun is known as the solar wind. Their interactions help drive space weather. On Earth, the effects can appear as auroras, while strong solar storms can disrupt satellites, positioning systems, radio communications, and power grids.
In this simulation of the Earth’s magnetic field, the solar wind is coming from the right-hand side of the image and Kelvin–Helmholtz waves are visible at the top. The color indicates the density of the plasma. Credit: Lauri Holappa / University of Oulu
Waves that satellites rarely see
The boundary waves are known as Kelvin–Helmholtz waves. Similar patterns sometimes appear in clouds, and related phenomena occur in the Sun’s atmosphere, along the edges of other planets’ magnetic fields, and in interstellar space. Around Earth, however, satellites rarely pass through the most active regions.
Those limited encounters have made it difficult to establish how the waves behave under different solar wind conditions, so the researchers used computer models of the entire magnetosphere to examine their formation.
Kelvin–Helmholtz waves can also be seen in a river’s current. A counter-current meets the main current, causing eddies and Kelvin–Helmholtz waves. A similar encounter between opposing currents occurs at the edge of the magnetosphere. Credit: Katariina Nykyri
“This finding grew out of a long process of thinking through what I was seeing. In 2020, when I was visiting NASA as a postdoctoral researcher, I noticed unusual simulation images of the magnetosphere. I later realized that they showed Kelvin–Helmholtz waves at the edge of the magnetosphere, and that the different behavior of the waves on different sides was part of the same phenomenon,” says Academy Research Fellow Lauri Holappa from the University of Oulu.
Magnetic fields weaken waves unevenly
The models traced the uneven wave activity to the way the solar wind’s magnetic field meets Earth’s field. Rather than wrapping evenly around the magnetosphere, the solar wind’s field drapes asymmetrically around it. This draped field can dampen the waves, but its damping effect varies from place to place, allowing stronger wave activity in some regions than in others.
“Asymmetries in the wave motion at the edge of the magnetic field have been observed before, but now we were able to show how they arise,” Holappa says.
The strongest activity appeared in the winter hemisphere, which faces away from the Sun. Within that hemisphere, the direction of the solar wind’s magnetic field determined whether the waves were concentrated on the dawn side or the dusk side.
Reference: “IMF By-Controlled Dawn–Dusk and Hemispheric Asymmetries of Kelvin–Helmholtz Waves and Reconnection Geometry Under Negative Dipole Tilt” by L. Holappa, K. Nykyri, J. Laitinen and B. Burkholder, 16 September 2026,
Geophysical Research Letters
DOI: 10.1029/2026GL124835

title: Earth’s Ice Ages May Have Started With a Planet-Wide Ocean Domino Effect
content:
Earth has experienced numerous ice ages throughout its history, when global temperatures fell and vast ice sheets expanded across large portions of the Northern Hemisphere. These prolonged cold periods were influenced by changes in Earth’s orbit, atmospheric carbon dioxide levels, and ocean circulation. Credit: Shutterstock
New research suggests that cooling in the Northern Hemisphere may have triggered far-reaching ocean changes that helped drive Earth’s past ice ages.
Growing ice sheets in the Northern Hemisphere may have helped push Earth into past ice ages by triggering changes in ocean circulation thousands of miles away, near Antarctica. New research from the University of St Andrews identifies a possible mechanism connecting these distant regions, helping explain how the planet naturally reduced atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO
) as ice ages developed.
Scientists have long known that the Southern Ocean plays a central role in regulating atmospheric CO
. Changes in its circulation and sea ice can increase the amount of carbon stored in the deep ocean, contributing to the cooling associated with ice ages. But researchers have struggled to explain how expanding northern ice sheets could influence waters so far south.
How Northern Ice Sheets Could Transform the Southern Ocean
The growth of massive Northern Hemisphere ice sheets begins with changes in Earth’s orbit that alter how solar energy is distributed across the planet. According to the new study, published in the
Journal of Climate
, these expanding ice sheets may set off a much larger chain of events by cooling nearby North Atlantic waters.
As those colder waters move through the global ocean circulation system, they can eventually reach the Southern Ocean. If the northern cooling is strong enough, it could alter circulation around Antarctica and promote conditions that allow more CO
to remain stored in the ocean rather than the atmosphere.
This proposed connection provides a physical explanation for how ice sheet growth in one hemisphere could help amplify cooling across the planet.
Ocean Simulations Reveal a Powerful Cooling Effect
To test the hypothesis, researchers used computer simulations that cooled only the ocean’s northernmost latitudes (mimicking the effect of a large ice sheet). They then examined whether the temperature changes could travel south and alter Southern Ocean conditions in ways that reduce atmospheric CO
The results showed that cooling northern waters alone produced a substantial response. The simulated reduction in atmospheric CO
reached 74% of the reduction produced when the researchers cooled the entire planet.
The experiments support the proposed connection between Northern Hemisphere ice sheets and Southern Ocean carbon storage. However, they demonstrate that the mechanism is physically plausible in a model, rather than establishing exactly how much it contributed to individual ice ages in Earth’s past.
Rethinking What Drives Earth’s Ice Ages
Lead author Dr. Madison Shankle, from the University of St Andrews’ School of Earth and Environmental Science, explained:
“Essentially, we’ve produced evidence of a plausible mechanism connecting these two far-flung puzzles pieces – Northern Hemisphere ice sheets and Southern Hemisphere ocean circulation changes leading to CO
drawdown – which has been a tricky thing to explain in our theory of Earth’s past ice ages. Our study takes the step of actually demonstrating them working in model simulations, which is a big step forward for this field.”
Ice age research has traditionally emphasized processes occurring around Antarctica, where ocean circulation strongly influences the exchange of carbon between the atmosphere and deep ocean. The new findings suggest that temperature changes in distant northern waters may also be an important part of that system.
Past ice ages provide natural examples of how carbon moves between Earth’s atmosphere and oceans over long periods. Understanding these processes can help scientists improve climate models and investigate how the global carbon cycle responds to changes in atmospheric CO
, including the additional carbon dioxide released by human activities.
Reference: “Isolated Northern Hemisphere Cooling in an Idealized Model Promotes Ocean Carbon Storage and Glacial-like Ocean Features” by Madison G. Shankle, Graeme A. MacGilchrist, Andrea Burke, Alice Marzocchi, Malte F. Jansen and James W. B. Rae, 22 October 2026,
Journal of Climate
DOI: 10.1175/JCLI-D-25-0355.1

title: Antarctica’s “Doomsday Glacier” Could Raise Sea Levels Twice As Much as Scientists Feared
content:
A photo taken during a Korea Polar Research Institute expedition in 2026 shows icebergs calving at a steady pace from the front of Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica. UC Irvine and NASA JPL scientists have developed a new computer model that incorporates accurate information about the glacier’s grounding zone, a kilometers-wide area beneath the ice that is coming into contact with warm ocean water. The researchers say this dynamic is causing twice as much ice melting and sea level rise as previously thought. Credit: David and Denise Holland / New York University
Even without further warming, Thwaites Glacier could contribute twice as much to sea level rise by 2100 as previously estimated, according to a revised ice sheet model.
Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica has been retreating and thinning rapidly, while satellites show substantial acceleration in its ice flow. Traditional ice sheet models have depicted slower movement, leaving scientists struggling to reconcile their simulations with the observations. The glacier lies in the Amundsen Sea Embayment, a sector responsible for roughly one-third of the Antarctic Ice Sheet’s mass loss.
A new ice sheet model developed by glaciologists at the University of California, Irvine and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory projects that melting at Thwaites could contribute up to 30 millimeters, or about 1.2 inches, to sea level rise by 2100. That is twice previous estimates, even without additional climate warming. The study was published in
Nature Communications
Warm seawater reaches beneath grounded ice
“Glaciologists have long based their assumptions of ice sheet dynamics on the ‘grounding line,’ a discreet, narrow and mostly stable demarcation where ice leaves the land and begins floating on water,” said lead author Mattia Poinelli, who was a UC Irvine postdoctoral scholar in Earth system science when the study was conducted. “We have come to acknowledge a different arrangement beneath Earth’s major ocean-terminating glaciers. Satellite observations demonstrate the existence of a ‘grounding zone,’ sometimes kilometers wide, where warm ocean water is reaching deep underneath the ice sheets and causing vigorous melting.”
Synthetic aperture radar readings from the Finnish ICEYE satellite constellation allowed the researchers to detect kilometer-scale fluctuations in this zone along the main trunk of Thwaites. The data indicate that seawater penetrates several kilometers beneath grounded ice and lifts it during tidal cycles. This flushes the underside of the ice with pressurized, warm seawater, which currents altered by climate change push toward the Antarctic coastline.
That contact with the ocean affects how firmly the glacier remains anchored to ridges on the seafloor. According to Poinelli, a NASA JPL research affiliate who is now a project scientist at UCLA, the study showed that grounding zone processes accelerate the glacier’s detachment from these stabilizing features, allowing faster ice flow and deterioration.
“The Thwaites main trunk is being temporarily stabilized by the Mouginot Ridge,” he said. “Once that ridge is unpinned, the glacier will continually retreat across a predominantly retrograde seafloor toward its next topographic high, the South Ridge.”
A retrograde seafloor slopes downward farther inland, so retreat would carry the glacier into deeper water before it reaches the next rise in the terrain.
A 60 percent chance of detachment
The researchers calibrated their model against more than 20 years of observations. By including a grounding zone instead of a grounding line, they reconstructed changes in the glacier from the 1990s to the present that were four times as pronounced as those represented in traditional models.
Simulations incorporating a grounding zone 4 to 6 kilometers wide, or about 2.5 to 3.7 miles, predict a 60 percent probability that the glacier will lose its anchoring contact with Mouginot Ridge by the end of the century, Poinelli said. “When you factor in key physical processes and calibrate against historical observations, you gain a reliable pathway for narrowing uncertainty in projections,” he said.
“We have documented and quantified the impacts of climate change on our planet’s sensitive ice sheets for decades, but a mounting realization gained in recent years of what is happening on the undersides of glaciers like Thwaites is leading to an even greater sense of alarm,” said co-author Eric Rignot, UC Irvine professor of Earth system science. “Most projections up-to-present have struggled to match the rapidity of the mass loss because of missing physics; our new model with more complete physics is able to match the record and then produces projections that are twice larger than before. These results predict greater risk of and exposure for coastal flooding than anticipated in the coming decades.”
Reference: “Sea-level contribution from Thwaites Glacier doubles in an observation-constrained ice-sheet model” by Mattia Poinelli, Eric Rignot, Hélène Seroussi, Joshua Cuzzone, Tyler Pelle and Eric Larour, 12 October 2026,
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77976-1

title: Mysterious Brain Signal Linked to Several Schizophrenia Symptoms
content:
Schizophrenia is a serious mental health disorder that affects how people think, perceive reality, and interact with the world. Symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking, and difficulties with communication. According to the World Health Organization, schizophrenia affects approximately 23 million people worldwide, or roughly 1 in every 345 people. Credit: Shutterstock
A weakened brain signal may offer new clues about schizophrenia and its earliest warning signs.
Schizophrenia affects how people perceive their surroundings, organize their thoughts, and communicate with others. Although these symptoms are often studied separately, new research suggests they may be connected to a common disruption in brain activity.
In a study published in
Science Advances
, scientists identified changes in a brain rhythm known as beta-band activity that were associated with several symptoms of schizophrenia. Patients with the most pronounced changes also had greater difficulty processing sensory information, more disorganized speech, and more severe clinical symptoms.
A Common Brain Signal Behind Different Symptoms
Researchers examined brain activity in 25 people with schizophrenia and 25 healthy participants using high-resolution magnetoencephalography, or MEG. The recordings were collected at the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre at the Montreal Neurological Institute-Hospital (The Neuro). Participants completed a task involving the timing of sights and sounds, and researchers separately analyzed their speech for signs of disorganization.
Compared with the control group, participants with schizophrenia showed weaker and slower beta-band activity. These brain rhythms are involved in processes that help the brain interpret sensory information and coordinate responses to the environment.
“What struck us was that the same weakened brain signal kept showing up wherever we looked, whether patients were processing a sound, a sight or completing a movement,” said Hsi (Tiana) Wei, lead author of the study and a postdoctoral scholar in
McGill University’s Department of Psychiatry and the Douglas Research Centre
. “Seeing the same pattern across these different domains suggested there may be a common underlying process linking the symptoms.”
The study relied on high-resolution MEG imaging carried out at the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre at the Montreal Neurological Institute-Hospital (The Neuro). Credit: Stephan Ballard
What the Findings Could Mean for Early Detection
The results support the possibility that some schizophrenia symptoms arise from disturbances in how the brain constructs and updates its understanding of the world. Rather than representing entirely independent problems, difficulties with perception, behavior, and speech may share an underlying neurological process.
“This gives us early but compelling evidence that measuring the brain’s operations, especially how it builds and revises its own model of the world, may help us appreciate that there is a common thread behind the confusing array of symptoms we see in disorders like schizophrenia,” said Dr. Lena Palaniyappan, senior author of the study, Professor of Psychiatry at McGill University, and director of the Centre of Excellence in Youth Mental Health at the Douglas Hospital.
Palaniyappan believes that further research could eventually help clinicians identify young people who need additional mental health support before psychosis develops. “The very first sign of schizophrenia begins in our adolescence, but this often gets missed for a long time. If this finding is confirmed in larger samples, we may have a potentially useful method to identify who, among youth seeking help for mental health, needs extra support to prevent psychosis,” he said.
Further Research Is Needed Before Clinical Use
The study involved just 50 participants, and its findings establish associations rather than demonstrating that altered beta-band activity causes schizophrenia symptoms. The researchers also have not established whether measuring this signal can reliably predict psychosis.
“This is a first, modest-size study, and the associations with speech and clinical severity will need to be tested in larger independent samples before we can be confident in them,” Wei said.
If future studies confirm the findings, beta-band activity could potentially serve as a measurable indicator of brain dysfunction associated with schizophrenia. Wei also suggested that the signal may be worth investigating as a future treatment target, although its clinical usefulness remains unproven.
Reference: “Neurophysiological dynamics related to perception, action, and language in schizophrenia” by Hsi T. Wei, Dominic Boutet, Rukun Dou, Jessica Ahrens, Nadia Zeramdini, Alban Voppel, Fernando Gonzales-Aste, Fatme Abboud, Sylvain Baillet and Lena Palaniyappan, 21 October 2026,

title: Scientists Discover That Ovaries May Be Doing Something Unexpected Decades After Menopause
content:
The ovaries are essential organs in the female reproductive system, responsible for producing eggs and hormones such as estrogen and progesterone. Although their reproductive function ends with menopause, emerging research suggests they remain biologically active and may continue to influence aging and overall health. Credit: Shutterstock
Ovaries often dismissed as inactive after menopause may still shape how women age, with human tissue revealing inflammatory changes and molecular similarities to ovarian cancer.
Ovaries continue to change for decades after menopause, long after their role in reproduction has ended. In a study of ovarian tissue from 28 women ages 50 to 75, scientists found age-related shifts in proteins associated with inflammation, immune activity, and the structure of the tissue surrounding cells.
The research, conducted by scientists at Northwestern University and the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, was published in
Aging Cell
“In the ovary, we reach a point of no return with respect to fertility in which it’s no longer producing eggs, and I would venture to say most people assume those ovaries are just sitting there doing nothing, similar to the appendix,” said co-corresponding author Francesca Duncan, associate professor of reproductive science in medicine at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. “But that’s what makes this study very different.”
Older ovaries show an inflammatory shift
To investigate what changes after menopause, the researchers looked beyond ovarian hormones to examine the tissue’s protein composition. Co-corresponding author Birgit Schilling, professor and director of the Mass Spectrometry Center at the Buck Institute, led the team responsible for that analysis. Spearheaded by Buck Institute staff scientist and Schilling lab member Mark Watson, the work used advanced proteomic technologies that can identify and measure thousands of proteins at once. The researchers analyzed 5,812 groups of proteins in normal ovarian tissue.
Headshot of co-corresponding author Birgit Schilling. Credit: Buck Institute for Research on Aging
Human ovarian tissue is difficult to obtain, making the collection of 28 ovaries unusually valuable, Duncan said. Concentrating on a 25-year age range after menopause allowed the team to isolate differences within the postmenopausal years, rather than comparing young and old ovaries across an entire lifespan. The technology also made it possible to examine thousands of proteins in every sample.
“When we analyzed the data in multiple different statistical ways, what became clear across all these methodologies is that the ovary was not stagnant,” Schilling said. “In fact, over the decades, there were quite dramatic differences in terms of some proteins’ levels would go up with age and some proteins’ levels would go down, which tells us this organ is quite dynamic.”
Ovaries from younger postmenopausal women contained more proteins involved in maintaining cells and tissue structure. Older ovaries had more proteins associated with inflammation, immune activity, and the breakdown and rebuilding of the tissue around cells. The differences were greatest between women in their 50s and those ages 70 and older.
Some of the molecular patterns also resembled those seen in cellular senescence. In this state, aging or damaged cells stop dividing but remain biologically active and can send signals that affect nearby tissue.
“Our data points to progressive aging features in which the ovary appears to lose its original identity and ends up doing something different,” Duncan said. “We do not yet know if there’s ever a point in a woman’s life when this organ is no longer beneficial and it’s actually harmful. These results really point to the need to ask this question.”
Similar remodeling in mice and women
Duncan’s group had previously found similar evidence of continued remodeling in
postmenopausal ovaries of mice
. She began both that research and the human study with expectations that the findings ultimately challenged.
“I was predicting that if we took a 50-year-old ovary, a 60-year-old ovary, a 70-year-old, an 80-year-old ovary, they would all look exactly the same, have no eggs, and basically be non-functional,” Duncan said. “The fact that across species we’re seeing this gives us confidence that this isn’t just some random event, but something truly meaningful is happening in the biology.”
Headshot of co-corresponding author Francesca Duncan. Credit: Northwestern University
Women now routinely live for decades after menopause, Duncan noted, making the ovary’s role during this long period increasingly relevant to understanding women’s health beyond fertility.
“The ovary is not just a reproductive organ,” Schilling said. “It really influences how somebody ages because it speaks to all these other organs, such as the brain, and also to the bone, and women after menopause experience often a lot of bone problems. So, we think there is a connection between all these organs.”
Cancer-linked proteins in cancer-free ovaries
The changes in tissue structure also connect the new findings to an earlier question about ovarian cancer. In 2016,
Duncan’s lab was the first to find
that aging ovaries become increasingly inflamed, fibrotic, and stiff, resembling scarring in other tissues. Cancer cells can thrive in stiff, collagen-rich environments, prompting the researchers to investigate whether these changes could make older ovaries more hospitable to cancer cells. The new protein analysis provides a molecular view of that remodeling process after menopause.
All the tissue in the current study appeared normal and cancer-free. Nevertheless, some proteins previously associated with ovarian cancer were more abundant in aging ovaries, with the strongest signal among women in their 60s. This does not mean the ovaries were cancerous or precancerous. It suggests that healthy ovarian aging and ovarian cancer share some biological processes.
“It’s not that all postmenopausal women get ovarian cancer, but we know that that fibrotic inflammatory environment is certainly an environment that cancer cells prefer to home in on,” Duncan said. “This is all consistent with the idea that the aging ovary is a potential third hit for ovarian cancer, with the first hit being genetic and the second hit being environmental. So can we target the aging ovary therapeutically to lower the risk of ovarian cancer, or can we develop novel biomarkers of ovarian cancer?”
Whether aging in the ovary can drive changes elsewhere in the body remains an open question.
“Is the ovary the canary in the coal mine in women?” said Duncan, who is also an associate professor in residence at the Buck Institute. “Could aging in the ovary set off a cascade of changes that continues throughout the body as women get older?”
The findings do not answer whether healthy ovaries should ever be removed after menopause, the researchers emphasized. Much more research is needed to determine exactly what the organ does during these years and whether the changes observed contribute to chronic disease or are simply features of normal aging.
Reference: “The Human Ovary Exhibits Dynamic Molecular Remodeling in the Decades Post-Menopause” by Mark A. Watson, Bikem Soygur, Christina D. King, Pooja R. Devrukhkar, Simon Melov, Elisheva D. Shanes, Mary Ellen G. Pavone, Francesca E. Duncan and Birgit Schilling, 7 September 2026,
Aging Cell
DOI: 10.1111/acel.70714

title: Snakebites Are Far Deadlier Than We Thought, New Study Reveals
content:
Millions of people worldwide suffer venomous snakebites each year, but many cases never appear in official health records. Credit: Shutterstock
Even fatal snakebites can go uncounted, and a model estimating up to 513,000 deaths annually could help direct lifesaving antivenom to communities that health records miss.
Not every snakebite injects venom. When venom enters the body, however, it can cause snake envenoming. This is a potentially fatal condition, and it mostly affects poor rural communities across tropical and subtropical regions who don’t have easy access to
medical care
As researchers with decades of combined experience in snakebite and tropical disease epidemiology, we came to realize that snake envenoming faces a data crisis. Over half of the countries where venomous snakes pose a threat don’t keep count of how many people are bitten or envenomed.
In rural sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia, many victims live hours away from the nearest clinic, lack transport, or seek care from
traditional healers
. As a result, their cases are never captured in national health statistics.
To bridge this massive gap, we conducted a
to map the global burden of snake envenoming and related deaths.
We looked at data from 79 countries by reviewing studies published up to 31 March 2025. This allowed us to update the findings from our milestone
2008 global burden study
. To fill the remaining data gaps, we built a geostatistical model that combines real-world data with local environmental and socioeconomic factors. This allowed us to estimate envenoming and fatality rates.
We conclude from our findings that snake envenoming is a public health crisis on a far greater scale than official statistics have shown. Our results show that sub-Saharan Africa bears the heaviest toll.
The World Health Organization has set an ambitious target to halve snakebite mortality and disability
. Mapping the problem at the country level is the first crucial step.
Uncovering the hidden burden
To overcome the lack of reliable data, we turned to a model-based geostatistics framework.
To understand how this modelling works, think of it as predicting invisible patterns by combining known data points with environmental signals. Instead of assuming data for every region, this modelling uses statistical probability to calculate a range of likely outcomes based on environmental signals.
We fed our model with data including climate, snake species richness, and socioeconomic indicators. The model then calculated the probability of snakebites occurring in specific locations, even where official health records were completely blank.
Egyptian Saw scaled Viper. Credit: Bernard DUPONT/Wikimedia Comons
Based on this, we estimate that at least 2.1 million people experience snake envenoming each year globally. The true number could be high as 7 million. Using our model, which adjusts for substantial under-reporting, annual deaths may range from 274,000 to 513,000.
The geographic distribution of this burden is uneven. Our research shows that sub-Saharan Africa alone accounts for 45% of all global envenomings and fatalities. That burden has likely been underestimated for decades. People in sub-Saharan Africa experience snake envenoming and death at nearly three times the rate seen in south Asia.
Countries like Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Ethiopia face a
high burden
, driven by dense rural populations and high exposure in agricultural fields.
Why sub-Saharan Africa is hit hardest
The reasons sub-Saharan Africa suffers such disproportionate harm are structural rather than accidental.
Firstly, the continent hosts a rich diversity of medically
important venomous species
. These include saw-scaled vipers (
spp.), puff adders (
Bitis arietans
), African cobras (
spp.), and mambas (
Dendroaspis
spp.). They are responsible for substantial morbidity and mortality across the continent.
Secondly, millions of rural agricultural workers labor in open fields without protective boots and walk on unlit footpaths at night. When a bite occurs, fragile health systems, long travel distances to regional facilities, and the high-cost or total absence of effective antivenom mean a treatable medical emergency can quickly become fatal. Similar conditions exist in parts of Asia.
We estimate that over 800,000 survivors are left with long-term physical disabilities each year, including amputations and other permanent impairments. These disabilities can reduce household income, increase healthcare costs, and push already vulnerable farming families deeper into poverty.
Going forward
Meeting the World Health Organization’s goal requires moving away from guesswork and using spatial risk data to guide real-world policy.
Snake envenoming has remained hidden for too long. Better data cannot solve the problem, but can help ensure that antivenom, healthcare services, and prevention efforts reach the communities that need them most.

title: Scientists Studied 865 Humpback Whales and Found They Grow Faster Than Expected
content:
Eastern Australian humpback whales are a migratory population that travels thousands of miles each year between feeding grounds in Antarctica and warmer breeding waters along Australia’s eastern coast. Credit: Shutterstock
Despite decades of environmental change and population recovery, eastern Australian humpback whales appear to have maintained their historical adult size.
Eastern Australian humpback whales grow at an extraordinary pace, reaching approximately 10.9 meters (35.8 feet) in length by age five. By six or seven years old, they have already attained about 90 percent of their eventual adult body length, according to new research led by Griffith University.
The findings, published in
Marine Mammal Science
, suggest these whales grow faster than humpback populations studied elsewhere. “This is faster growth than other humpback whale populations that have been measured,” said lead researcher Stephanie Stack, a Griffith University PhD candidate.
Drones Reveal How Quickly Humpback Whales Grow
To investigate how humpbacks develop throughout their lives, researchers measured 865 individually identified whales between 2021 and 2024. Using drones to photograph the animals from above, they calculated body lengths without physically disturbing the whales. Long-term photo-identification records helped the team track growth across newborn calves, juveniles, and adults more than 40 years old.
The measurements showed that humpbacks experience their fastest growth during early life, with the rate gradually declining as they approach adult size. Including calves and young whales allowed scientists to examine these crucial developmental stages directly rather than relying on estimates derived from older animals.
The study’s findings suggested eastern Australian humpback whales grew faster than other humpback whale populations studied elsewhere in the world. Credit: Pacific Whale Foundation
Replacing Decades-Old Whaling Data
“These are also the first contemporary growth curves developed for eastern Australian humpback whales using measurements from living animals, updating knowledge that has relied heavily on measurements collected during the commercial whaling era in the mid-20th century,” Stack said.
Eastern Australia’s humpback population has recovered dramatically since commercial whaling ended, becoming one of the world’s most successful examples of whale conservation. Despite this population rebound and decades of environmental change, the new measurements closely match historical estimates of adult humpback size in Australian waters.
“These new growth curves establish a baseline for investigating how whale biology may respond to changing environmental conditions.”
Understanding Whale Health in a Changing Ocean
“Understanding how quickly whales grow provides another piece of the puzzle in understanding the biology of this recovering population,” Stack said. “Growth influences many aspects of a whale’s life, including its health, energy requirements and potentially the timing of reproduction.”
The new growth curves provide researchers with a reference point for tracking possible changes in humpback development as ocean conditions shift. Future measurements could help determine whether environmental changes are affecting growth patterns in this recovering population.
“As environmental conditions continue to change, having robust biological benchmarks like these will be essential for understanding how whale populations are responding,” Stack said.
Reference: “Contemporary Growth Curves for Individual Humpback Whales in Eastern Australia Using Aerial Photogrammetry” by S. H. Stack, T. Fettermann, B. McGovern and S. M. Bengtson Nash, 15 October 2026,
Marine Mammal Science

title: Physicists Use Light To Unlock a Crystal’s Hidden Electrical Powers
content:
Researchers at Auburn University have discovered that brief laser pulses can create electrical order inside a crystal at temperatures where its tiny polar regions normally remain disorganized. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
A crystal’s laser-induced electrical order lasts just a trillionth of a second, giving researchers a way to explore ultrafast approaches to processing and storing information.
Inside a crystal, tiny electrical regions can point in different directions or line up in an organized pattern. Cooling helps bring them into alignment, but physicists at
Auburn University
have now shown that brief flashes of laser light can also produce order at warmer temperatures, where those regions would otherwise remain disorganized.
The team worked with single crystals of a modified form of strontium titanate. The material allows electrons to move through it while also containing tiny regions with distinct positive and negative sides, an unusual combination of electrical properties. These regions are known as polar nanoregions.
Cooling aligns existing polar regions
For decades, physicists have debated whether atoms shift together to create the material’s polarized state or whether its polar regions already exist and become organized as it cools. Telling those explanations apart has been difficult because the regions are so small and their signals so faint.
Wencan Jin, the Thomas and Jean Walter Endowed Associate Professor in Auburn’s Department of Physics, led the research with graduate student Mohamed Kandil. The project began at the 2023 American Physical Society March Meeting, where Jin connected with researchers in Japan who could grow the crystals. Collaborators at Japan’s National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology grew the samples used in the experiments.
The Auburn researchers built a highly sensitive laser-based measurement system, then spent nearly a year improving the equipment before detecting the regions’ faint optical signal. By measuring how the crystal changed incoming light, they could track the regions’ alignment through repeated rounds of warming and cooling. The measurements showed disordered directions at higher temperatures giving way to preferred orientations as the crystal cooled. This provided strong evidence that the polar regions were already present before they lined up.
A picosecond of laser-induced order
The team still had to capture the fleeting moment when laser illumination brought the regions into alignment. “The breakthrough came in 2025, when Mohamed finally observed the disordered polar regions becoming aligned under laser illumination,” Jin said. “Seeing that signal emerge was a thrilling moment for the team.”
The light-induced alignment lasted only a picosecond, or one trillionth of a second (10⁻¹² second), but an optical measurement could still detect the resulting pattern. Being able to create and read that brief arrangement with light gives researchers a way to investigate extremely fast approaches to processing and storing information. It also provides a tool for studying electrical behavior that is otherwise difficult to observe.
“This experiment has truly been Mohamed’s odyssey,” Jin said. “It took him three years of dedication to complete the work and achieve his first publication.”
Reference: “Optical Poling of a Quantum Ferroelectric Metal across the Order-Disorder Phase Transition” by Mohamed Kandil, Yasuhide Tomioka, Yafei Ren, Ryan Comes, Isao H. Inoue and Wencan Jin, 14 October 2026,
Physical Review Letters

title: Archaeologists May Have Just Discovered the World’s Oldest Shipwreck
content:
Divers transport material discovered during the research. Credit: Hakan Öniz
Jars from what may be the world’s oldest shipwreck still hold visible residues, offering a chance to identify what Mediterranean traders carried around 4,500 years ago.
A shipwreck off the coast of Turkey is the oldest shipwreck in the world, our team of archaeologists believes.
There’s little left of the ship itself but based on clues from its cargo—including pottery vessels—a research team I was part of has tentatively dated the wreck to around 2700–2400 BCE.
That’s about 4,500 years ago. Prior to this discovery, the world’s oldest shipwreck was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, in Greece, thought to have been from about 4,200 years ago.
Much work remains to be done to refine the conclusions, and a paper outlining the results is yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal. Yet the discovery could transform our understanding of ancient Mediterranean connections during the Early Bronze Age.
Here, and perhaps even earlier, lie the foundations of extensive trade routes as we know them today.
Searching for clues
Associate Professor Hakan Öniz of Akdeniz University, Antalya, has worked along this coastline for decades excavating ancient shipwrecks.
Acting on clues from local seafarers, Öniz found a shipwreck in shallow waters off Kekova, west of Antalya in Turkey,
. Earlier this year, he contacted me and asked if I would help date some of the pottery vessels found on this wreck.
As an archaeologist specializing in desert sites, this was a singular experience. New technology, waterlogged methods of excavation, and laborious conservation techniques were the new normal. Yet there is always room for learning new skills in life.
Of the ship itself, there is now nothing to see, owing to underwater exposure. Yet the research team has now estimated the ship and its cargo dates to around 2700–2400 BCE. However, the precise dating is still under consideration. Earlier or later dates on either side of this initial determination are also possible.
A time capsule of ancient trade
This discovery promises to rewrite our understanding of early trade networks from around 4,500 years ago.
The ship is a “missing piece” in the story of networks, trade, and commodity exchange in the wider eastern Mediterranean. This era includes the Pyramid Age of Giza and its mighty pharaohs.
What remains under the sea is a time capsule of ancient trade.
Ancient pottery recovered from a shipwreck off Turkey could reveal surprising details about Bronze Age maritime trade.  Credit: Hakan Öniz
Although its direction was not known, the boat was evidently travelling along the coast of southern Turkey.
Now resting on the seabed between two islands, it is apparent the ship likely sought refuge in the lee waters during a storm. One could imagine the terror of the sailors—possibly coastal people from the Levant region—as their ship crashed against the rocks.
While timbers from the ship disappeared long ago, the remains of its precious cargo were embedded in the rocky slope along the Kekova coast.
Divers worked over the past four months to extract its pottery from barnacles clinging to the rocky underwater slope.
A closer look at pottery
Pottery is like plastic: it never goes away and just breaks down into smaller and smaller pieces.
Yet humble pottery vessels hold many clues about the past.
In this case, the cargo included large ceramic storage vessels, or amphorae, which once contained products from regions of the eastern Mediterranean.
The pots were large ovoid, flat-based jars with two handles, many featuring a raised horizontal clay “belt” around the widest part of the jar.
Through these vessels, it was possible to ascertain many pieces of information. This includes the likely origin of the jars and the contents exchanged across the region.
Importantly, the shape and manufacturing technique of the pots themselves help us date the cargo. By extension, this includes also the date of other pottery, and the ship itself.
The bigger picture
Compared to later periods, trade, and exchange in the eastern Mediterranean during the third millennium (3000–2000 BCE) is poorly understood.
Maritime voyages during the that period are known from Egyptian texts, pottery vessels, and raw materials from ancient tombs.
Around the same time as this ship struck the rocks, the ancient Egyptians were trading in the eastern Mediterranean through the port of Byblos in Lebanon.
Commodities such as cedar, tin/lead, oils, tree resins, lapis lazuli, and silver, all materials that Egypt lacked, were imported by the Egyptian state.
Recent scientific
research
also reveals that silver was acquired by the Egyptian state around 2600 BCE.
Analyses
showed this silver was acquired from the Lavrion mines east of modern Athens.
While it is unlikely Egyptian ships made this journey, boats like the Kekova ship may have used the route as part of an extended international maritime network.
And what was in the jars? Remarkably, there were still residues visible to the naked eye. Again, scientific analyses are pending, but could be some of the products mentioned in the Egyptian texts, possibly olive oil, wine, or tree resin.
The ship may have acquired its pottery from several ports on their journey. Our best assessment at this stage of research is that some of the “belted” jars (or clays used to make them) may have originated in the Central Jordan Valley.
The coast of southern Turkey is littered with ancient shipwrecks. While maritime archaeology is a relatively recent phenomenon, some of the world’s most famous wrecks have been discovered there. Who knows what other secrets these waters hold?

title: Dementia Will Cost America a Staggering $818 Billion This Year
content:
Millions of Americans provide unpaid dementia care, creating an enormous but often overlooked economic burden. New research reveals how these hidden sacrifices contribute to the disease’s staggering national cost. Credit: Shutterstock
Lost quality of life accounts for the largest share of dementia’s estimated $818 billion U.S. toll, offering a broader measure of what better care could preserve.
Family members and friends caring for Americans with dementia provide billions of hours of unpaid help, often during their prime working years. Their time, lost earnings, and the physical and emotional strain of caregiving contribute to an economic burden that reaches far beyond medical bills.
A new study led by the
University of Southern California (USC)
estimates that Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias will cost the United States $818 billion in 2026, driven largely by costs borne by people living with dementia and those who care for them. The figure includes medical and long-term care spending alongside the estimated value of unpaid caregiving, forgone earnings, and diminished quality of life. These broader losses often go uncounted in other estimates of dementia’s economic toll.
As new care models help people with dementia stay at home longer while supporting their families, the distribution of care costs could change. New therapies are also slowing Alzheimer’s, and FDA-approved blood tests can detect the disease before symptoms appear.
“Remarkable innovations can alter the trajectory of dementia in the United States if they are used effectively,” said Dana Goldman, founding director of the USC Schaeffer Institute. “The evidence we are building on dementia costs will provide the healthcare system with a clearer understanding of these and future innovations.”
Total cost of dementia by cost category. Credit: USC Schaeffer Center for Health Policy & Economics
Dementia’s largest cost is lost well-being
Understanding those changes requires accounting for both the money spent on care and the losses absorbed by patients and families. The study, published in
Alzheimer’s & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer’s Association
, estimates the following for 2026:
Dementia population: An estimated 5.7 million Americans are living with dementia, including 5.1 million ages 65 and older.
Quality of life: Declines in cognition, function, and independence among people with dementia account for $320 billion in estimated quality-of-life losses, the largest component of the total cost. Informal care partners experience an additional $15 billion in losses related to emotional and physical strain.
Unpaid caregiving: About 5.2 million people provide 6.8 billion hours of unpaid care for family members or friends with dementia. The model values that time at $237 billion.
Medical and long-term care: These costs total $222 billion. Medicare and Medicaid cover about 70%, or $154 billion, while patients and families pay 20%, or $46 billion, out of pocket.
Lost earnings: People with dementia and their care partners forgo a combined $23 billion in annual earnings.
These estimates come from the
U.S. Cost of Dementia Project
, a multiyear research effort funded through a cooperative agreement with the National Institute on Aging. Researchers build the model using large, nationally representative datasets, including the Health and Retirement Study and administrative health data from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
The accounting is still being refined. Following last year’s inaugural report, the researchers expanded the 2026 peer-reviewed estimates to include forgone earnings among people living with dementia and new models of health-related quality-of-life impacts on care partners. They also published a peer-reviewed
methods paper
this year to make their data, assumptions, and modeling accessible and transparent.
Forecasting who will bear dementia’s costs
Beyond calculating annual totals, the team uses dynamic microsimulation, a method that follows simulated individuals over time, to project how new treatments, care models, and policies could affect future dementia costs. Those projections include often-hidden consequences for well-being and finances. The project aims to provide the most comprehensive accounting yet of dementia’s economic impact, tracking changes in who bears the costs and when to inform policy and treatment decisions.
“By providing annual, comprehensive and transparent estimates of dementia’s total costs, our research can help guide decisions about how to allocate resources as the dementia population is set to grow substantially,” said lead researcher Julie Zissimopoulos, principal investigator of the U.S. Cost of Dementia Project, co-director of the Aging and Cognition program at the USC Schaeffer Center for Health Policy & Economics, and a professor at the USC Price School of Public Policy. “With our modeling approach, we can ask and answer questions such as: How will a new treatment that slows dementia improve quality of life or affect demand for nursing home care?”
Reference: “The cost of dementia in the United States in 2026” by Johanna Thunell, Bryan Tysinger, Matthew Baumgart, Maria Carrillo, Eileen Crimmins, Dana Goldman, Hanke Heun-Johnson, Mireille Jacobson, Geoff Joyce, Duncan Leaf, Lycia Tramujas Vasconcellos Neumann and Julie Zissimopoulos, 24 June 2026,
Alzheimer’s & Dementia
DOI: 10.1002/alz.71480
This work was funded through a cooperative agreement with the National Institute on Aging (U01AG086827).

title: Popular Sleep Supplement Could Come With an Unexpected Catch, Scientists Warn
content:
A popular cannabis-derived sleep supplement may affect the body in surprising ways. New research suggests its biological effects extend beyond sleep, with potential consequences that remain poorly understood. Credit: Shutterstock
A cannabis compound sold to help people sleep caused withdrawal symptoms in mice after just three days of repeated use.
Researchers at the
University of Connecticut
found that repeated doses of cannabinol, or CBN, produced tolerance and withdrawal symptoms in mice. The study, published in
Drug and Alcohol Dependence
, raises questions about a substance whose popularity as a sleep aid has outpaced research into its risks.
“CBN is everywhere right now. Gummies, tinctures, capsules, and it’s marketed as a safe, herbal sleep supplement,” says Steven Kinsey, a professor in UConn’s Elisabeth DeLuca School of Nursing. “Our findings suggest consumers should be aware repeated use may carry risks.”
CBN Shows Signs of Dependence
Like THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) and CBD (cannabidiol), CBN occurs naturally in cannabis. It is generally described as less psychoactive than THC, but the researchers found that it acts on some of the same biological systems involved in cannabis dependence.
Mice given CBN twice daily for three days developed tolerance, meaning the drug’s effects weakened with repeated exposure. They also displayed withdrawal signs when it was removed, including head twitches and paw fluttering that the researchers compared with trembling hands in people.
A separate experiment examined whether mice could distinguish CBN’s effects from those of THC. Animals trained to respond in a particular way after receiving THC responded similarly to CBN, suggesting the substances produced comparable internal cues. These findings suggest that milder intoxicating effects do not necessarily mean a lower risk of dependence.
Sleep Claims Outpace the Evidence
“The marketing of minor cannabinoids is pretty wild right now. There are so many therapeutic claims about these drugs, but we really don’t know much about their potential risks, especially with repeated use,” says lead author Olivia Vanegas, who earned her Ph.D. at UConn in 2026.
Although CBN is increasingly sold to help people sleep, little is known about the quality of that sleep or the consequences of regularly taking the doses used in sleep products.
Whether regular CBN use can lead to addiction remains unknown, but the history of sleep aids gives researchers a reason to investigate. Some drugs once promoted for a better night’s rest later proved dangerously habit-forming, making CBN’s unanswered safety questions harder to ignore.
Potential Benefits Need Closer Study
The researchers also observed anti-inflammatory effects at lower CBN doses that did not produce psychoactive effects in the mice. During a simulated bacterial challenge, however, CBN dampened the immune response, suggesting that its effects on inflammation could also influence the body’s defenses against infection.
Researchers still need to determine when CBN’s effects might be useful and when they might create risks. Kinsey emphasizes that the study involved mice, leaving substantial uncertainty about its effects in people, particularly at high doses or with prolonged use.
“CBN may still have therapeutic value,” he says. “But until we know more about dosing and long-term effects, the message for consumers is simple: buyer beware.”
Reference: “Tolerance, physical dependence, and Δ9-THC-like interoceptive effects of cannabinol in mice” by S.O. Vanegas, J.A. Marusich, J. Maturano, D. Sarlah and S.G. Kinsey, 6 September 2026,
Drug and Alcohol Dependence
DOI: 10.1016/j.drugalcdep.2026.113341

title: Researchers Find That Arthritis May Leave a Hidden Memory in Your Joints
content:
Arthritis is a common condition that causes inflammation, pain, stiffness, and swelling in the joints, affecting millions of people worldwide. Although its causes and symptoms vary, arthritis can significantly impact mobility and quality of life. Credit: Shutterstock
Arthritis may leave a memory in the joints, and mouse experiments suggest stress can reawaken it with help from the body’s heat-producing fat.
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) can flare in previously affected joints even after the disease has gone into remission. Psychological stress has long been associated with worsening symptoms, but how it might help inflammation return to those joints has remained unclear.
A study in mice now points to a chain of signals linking the nervous system, heat-producing fat, and cells in the joints. Blocking parts of that chain reduced stress-triggered arthritis in the animals, suggesting a possible direction for future treatments.
The study was led by Assistant Professor Shigeru Tanaka and Professor Hiroshi Nakajima at Chiba University in Japan, in collaboration with two Japanese hospitals. The findings were published in
Science Advances
on October 16, 2026.
Brown fat helps reignite joint inflammation
The researchers used a mouse model in which arthritis entered a remission-like state before the animals were exposed to restraint stress. Joint inflammation returned after that exposure. To trace the signals responsible, the team analyzed tissues, profiled immune cells, and measured molecular changes.
Stress activated the sympathetic nervous system, which helps coordinate the body’s stress response, and brown adipose tissue (BAT), a type of fat that produces heat. This activation prompted the brown fat to release interleukin-6 (IL-6), an inflammatory signaling protein. Circulating IL-6 then acted on fibroblast-like synoviocytes, specialized cells in the synovial tissue surrounding the joints.
In response, these joint cells produced CXCL1, a chemokine that attracts immune cells. CXCL1 drew in neutrophils, a type of white blood cell involved in inflammation, contributing to the return of arthritis.
“Our findings suggest that the effects of psychological stress on arthritis extend beyond the immune cells traditionally associated with autoimmune disease. Instead, stress can activate processes within other tissues that contribute to the return of joint inflammation,” Tanaka explains.
Blocking the pathway reduced arthritis flares
The team tested whether interrupting this sequence could reduce the flares by blocking key receptors and monitoring inflammatory markers, joint swelling, and immune-cell accumulation. Treating the mice with a β3-adrenergic receptor antagonist, a substance that blocks that receptor, reduced IL-6 levels in blood plasma, joint swelling, CXCL1 expression, and the accumulation of neutrophils in the joints. Blocking CXCR2, the receptor that responds to CXCL1, also significantly reduced stress-triggered arthritis in the mouse model.
The findings suggest that previously affected joint tissue may retain a form of inflammatory memory that stress can reactivate independently of lymphocytes, a group of immune cells. This offers a possible biological explanation for how inflammation can return to joints after arthritis has subsided.
A genetic clue in patients with RA
To examine whether the pathway might also be relevant to people, the researchers compared perceived stress and disease activity in patients with RA. Patients carrying Trp64Arg, a specific variant of the
gene that makes cells less responsive to stress-related hormones, showed a weaker relationship between perceived stress and arthritis activity than patients without the variant. The human analysis was observational, however, so it does not establish that stress directly caused changes in disease activity.
Understanding this pathway could eventually help researchers develop strategies to improve disease management and quality of life for people with RA. Its potential as a treatment target remains to be explored.
“Our findings suggest that targeting the stress-responsive pathways may offer a future therapeutic strategy that acts without broadly suppressing the immune system,” Nakajima notes.
Reference: “Fibroblast-like synoviocytes exacerbate autoimmune arthritis upon psychological stress in an IL-6–dependent manner” by Jun Tamura, Shigeru Tanaka, Keishi Etori, Daisuke Hashiba, Shuhei Kameda, Atsuko Tomikawa, Ryo Kikuchi, Tatsuro Takahashi, Aiko Saku, Hirotoshi Kawashima, Junichi Nakamura, Seiji Ohtori, Shin-Ichiro Kagami, Koichi Hirose and Hiroshi Nakajima, 16 October 2026,
Science Advances
DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aec9257
This work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI grant 23K07890 (Shigeru Tanaka), the Japan Science and Technology Agency (Moonshot R&D) grant JPMJMS2025 (Hiroshi Nakajima), and the Agency for Medical Research and Development (AMED)-SCARDA 223fa627003h0002 (Japan Initiative for World-leading Vaccine Research and Development Center, Chiba University, Synergy Institute for Futuristic Mucosal Vaccine Research and Development (cSIMVa)) (Hiroshi Nakajima).

title: INA Solar and Caelux sign 3 GW partnership for perovskite-TOPCon hybrid-tandem modules
content:
INA Solar and Caelux sign 3 GW partnership for perovskite-TOPCon hybrid-tandem modules
India’s Insolation Energy (INA Solar), through its subsidiary Insolation Green Energy, has reportedly signed a five-year strategic partnership with US-based
to commercialize 3 GW of advanced solar modules, according to a recent press release. The modules would combine Caelux’s Energy Producing Glass, a perovskite-based power-generating layer in the module’s top glass, with INA Solar’s N-type TOPCon cell platform.
The companies aim to develop “hybrid-tandem” modules and say commercial production could reach up to 29% module efficiency by 2028. They will work together on technology validation, manufacturing readiness and regulatory approvals, including India’s ALMM requirements. The release does not give a production start date or a delivery schedule.
INA Solar, based in Jaipur, Rajasthan, and listed on the NSE and BSE, operates three module factories in Jaipur with a combined capacity of 5.5 GW. It is developing a 4.5 GW TOPCon cell factory and an aluminum frame factory in Madhya Pradesh. Caelux said that with this agreement, its global contracted volume with module manufacturers exceeds 25 GW.
The agreement follows other five-year Caelux partnerships with Indian manufacturers, including
GREW Solar
(up to 4 GW) and
Rayzon Solar
(5 GW), as well as a 3 GW deal with US-based

title: Data Center Late Fees Hit $5 Million or More Per Day, Spawning New Insurance
content: This spring, Mike Mathews, who leads the global digital infrastructure practice at insurance broker Marsh, raced to design a policy to protect a data center developer from a $1 million-a-day late fee. The developer’s tenant was demanding damages if electricity and facilities weren’t available on time during the first phase of a new gigawatt-scale facility. Mathews’ team arranged the novel coverage, a bespoke form of “delay-in-delivery” coverage just for data centers, only to see penalties escalate sharply in a matter of months: Tenants in new deals began asking for upwards of $5 million for each day of delay, citing even higher estimates of lost revenue. Welcome to the wild, and no longer boring, world of insurance whisperers trying to keep data center developers alive. Marsh, one of the two leading insurance brokers alongside Aon, is designing policies for AI infrastructure risks where data can be scant and financial exposures are growing to a scale never contemplated. Bankers and bondholders are asking for more of this insurance to get comfortable underwriting record amounts of spending by first-time developers and money-losing AI startups. The recent quintupling of this type of late-delivery fee, and escalation of others, “sent a shockwave,” says Mathews. “I’m not saying investors were hands off on insurance, but they’re all hands on now.” Swiss Re estimates that data center insurance premiums could approach $24 billion by 2030. S&P Global estimates premiums are already running around $10 billion 2026, which is twice the size of the global aviation insurance market. Data center construction growth has been so rapid —now roughly $2 trillion in insurable value and growing $300 billion a year—that S&P warned in a recent report, “We expect capacity constraints to limit the industry’s ability to fully insure these hyperscale data center projects, as total insurable values reach $20 billion-$30 billion per location.” When every party in a buildout relies on borrowed money, a delay can create cascading problems. “My bet is late penalties will bankrupt more developers than interest rates ever will,” KKR’s global head of digital infrastructure, Waldemar Szlezak, wrote this month in a recap of a J.P. Morgan infrastructure investment forum. Mathews compares insurance to a clock: “Over the past 100 years, insurance has maybe changed five minutes. But if you look at digital and data centers, it spins like a stopwatch.” GPU Insurance Mathews has hired mostly data center development and operations veterans like himself, rather than career insurance brokers, to staff his team in recent years, and just brought on a former risk manager from Meta. They are helping insurers design coverage for emerging risks, including service interruptions caused by new types of equipment, potential declines in the value of Nvidia graphics processing units, and financial guarantees for multibillion-dollar utility upgrades, even when developers may not use the full power capacity. Efforts to insure the residual value of GPUs are still nascent, Mathews said. Older chips are holding their value or even rising in a scarce market, so pricing such protection is tricky. Meta said Marsh is its insurance broker on a data center project in El Paso, Texas. Marsh has cited its own role in arranging insurance solutions for Meta’s large AI campus in Monroe, Louisiana. Marsh recently said it found insurance providers for more than $5 billion in multiple forms of credit protection for a data center developer making long-term commitments to pay for utility infrastructure. Oracle has had to satisfy such commitments in Wisconsin, but Marsh did not identify its client. The AI risks that need insurance today do not fit neatly into the categories that builders and cloud providers have traditionally been able to insure. Conventional policies cover construction delays or business interruptions caused by physical events, such as fires or storm-related water damage. They did not cover the risk that a utility cannot provide power on a promised timeline or that an on-site power plant is delayed. Mathews offers an analogy: Imagine building or renovating a house that the developer promises will be ready by Christmas, only to find you must wait until February for appliances or a power hookup. That aggravating delay is usually tough luck—not an insurable event. If, after you move in, a leak or air-conditioning failure forces you out during repairs, it might be on you to spring for a few nights in a hotel. Annoying, but it won’t bankrupt you. Now imagine a data center firm that promises to hand over as much as a 1 GW powered data center shell to an AI developer or cloud provider, only to postpone delivery from Christmas to the end of February. Late fees of up to $5 million a day could consume the entire daily rental income that the facility’s landlord was expecting, says Christian Okoye of Occam Edge, which quantifies delay costs for investors, lenders and developers. Over those two months, the data center firm could owe $300 million in penalties while also forgoing rent—a damaging combination for loan repayments. And an AI lab could forgo multiples of that $300 million in monthly revenue if it can’t get its chips energized, as we recently reported , or if the data center goes down. Even for risks that are insurable, like storms, owners may make a business decision to only insure part of a gigawatt scale campus given that the facilities plus the pricey chips and servers cost around $50 to $60 billion per gigawatt. Mathews says he hasn’t found any project to be uninsurable and points out that reinsurers have excess capital they want to put to work in this market. Or, to satisfy bondholders, some developers may go above and beyond. The relatively young bitcoin-miner-turned-AI-infrastructure developer Hut 8 is building a data center in Corpus Christi, on the Gulf Coast of Texas where hurricanes are a regular risk. Sean Glennan, CFO of Hut 8, said “we went well above maximum and probable foreseeable loss on these policies…We said, ‘Let’s get very robust insurance policies to give bondholders peace of mind.’” Hut 8 also bought 19 months of “delay in startup” insurance to provide some revenue protection if insured damage causes a delay. And Glennan says he negotiated a lease that can’t be terminated if the Texas campus experiences certain delays. Hut 8 used the insurer FM and the broker Aon. Pooling Risk Marsh and Aon have both been arranging multibillion-dollar insurance facilities, which are arrangements where insurers pool risks across multiple projects. Pooled risks are necessary because no single insurer is set up to absorb tens of billions of dollars of risk on a single campus. Because portions of sites must be “self-insured or only partially insured,” S&P said in an April report that it expects growth in alternative arrangements like insurance-linked securities. Tim Walker, Marsh’s digital infrastructure construction leader, points out that some challenges just aren’t insurable. “What happens when you don’t have enough people to build all these things? To me that’s one of the biggest risks.” The demand just keeps getting bigger as penalties rise: RBC Capital Markets recently reported that a data center where temperatures deviated from safe targets for one month risked a $150 million penalty. A report by Gallagher Re found that a single 45-minute outage could wipe out 40% of a data center’s annual cash flow in penalties, if it is held to the traditional industry promise of 99.999% uptime, or about five minutes of downtime a year. An old risk, that rats could eat through data center-related cables, has re-surfaced as an even bigger worry. A certain fiber maker used to make a cable in a shade of orange that rats loved, leading to new insurance add-ons for “vermin.” Vermin could cost providers a whole lot more as they rush back into cities to serve up AI inferencing. “You can build a $10 billion, state-of-the-art facility, and Chuck E. title: 科学网-一周热闻回顾（2026年10月25日）
content:
一周热闻回顾（2026年10月25日）
教育部公布最新学位授权点动态调整及自主审核结果
教育部网站发布4则通知，分别是：《国务院学位委员会关于下达2026年度动态调整撤销和增设学位授予点名单的通知》《国务院学位委员会关于下达2025年度动态调整撤销和增设学位授予点名单的通知》《国务院学位委员会关于下达2026年度学位授予资格自主审核单位撤销和增设学位授予点名单的通知》《国务院学位委员会关于下达2025年度学位授予资格自主审核单位撤销和增设学位授予点名单的通知》。
王虹等4学者获2026年度“求是杰出科学家奖”
求是科技基金会（Qiu Shi Science & Technologies Foundation）官网公布了2026年度“求是杰出科学家奖”（数学与物理领域）获奖名单。
数学领域的2名获奖者为：
王国祯（复旦大学）：因其在同伦论及球面稳定同伦群计算方面的贡献入选，其中包括发展基模变形方法，以及解决克尔维尔不变量问题最后遗留的126维情形。
王虹（美国纽约大学、法国高等科学研究所）：因其在调和分析与几何测度论领域的贡献获得认可，包括在局部平滑、菲斯滕伯格集方面的开创性工作，特别是解决了三维挂谷猜想。
物理领域的2名获奖者为：
贾金锋（上海交通大学）：因在拓扑绝缘体制备、拓扑量子态中马约拉纳零能模探测，以及超导体奇异电子结构研究方面取得的突破性成果而获得高度认可。
叶军（美国科罗拉多大学博尔德分校）:因在开发高精度光晶格钟、推进基于该时钟的基础物理精密检验方面所作出的开创性贡献，以及在首个极性分子量子气体和超冷化学研究领域的成果而闻名。
我国新一代医用重离子加速器首台示范装置建成
基于中国科学院近代物理研究所成功研发的新一代超紧凑旋转束重离子治疗系统(SIMM)，中国国产新一代医用重离子加速器首台示范装置，近日在广东省惠州重离子医学中心建成。
目前，中国新一代超紧凑旋转束重离子治疗系统首台示范装置已进入设备检测阶段，预计将于2026年底开展临床试验。
这标志着中国精准放疗领域取得里程碑进展，有望推动高端医疗装备惠及更多肿瘤患者，促进中国离子放疗产业升级。
武汉大学领导班子调整
武汉大学官网“现任领导”一栏更新显示，朱德友已任武汉大学党委副书记、副校长。
朱德友，研究生学历。历任武汉测绘科技大学学生工作部副部长、学生处副处长兼就业工作办公室主任、武汉大学遥感信息工程学院党委副书记等职。
河海大学获捐1000万
10月23日，河海大学举行校友企业家捐赠仪式。校长郑金海出席仪式并致辞。2003级材料专业校友、江苏天之洁环境工程有限公司总经理陆涵军，2003级土木专业校友、江苏河海工程技术有限公司副总经理韦永耀参加捐赠仪式。
江苏天之洁环境工程有限公司、江苏河海工程技术有限公司分别向学校捐赠500万元，支持学校教育事业高质量发展。
兰州一高校学生参赛作品被指涉嫌抄袭，校方通报：已开展核查
兰州资源环境职业技术大学发布情况通报：
针对近日网络上对我校学生李某参加中国国际大学生创新大赛（2026）甘肃省分赛作品涉嫌抄袭的反映。学校高度重视，第一时间已组织相关部门对举报所涉事项开展核查，相关情况正在依规依程序核实处理中。
使用AI撰写论文的博士生不太可能留在学术界
据《自然》报道，一份未经同行评审的论文指出，美国科学、技术、工程和数学（STEM）领域的博士学位论文中，约30%包含由人工智能（AI）生成的文本。研究还发现，那些使用AI撰写论文的博士毕业生更有可能在工业界工作，而不太可能进入学术界。
多项研究表明，近年来，科学文献中使用AI生成的文本数量显著增加。美国国家经济研究局（NBER）的研究人员希望了解博士生是如何使用AI的。“如果我们的学生只做了一半的工作，另一半交给AI，那么他们是否具备成为优秀科学家所需的深度理解能力？”论文合著者、NBER的经济学家Daniel Gross说。
